2. In Writ Petition No.17056 of 2012, Rule Nisi has been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned Memos, bearing No. BR Dhaka No. 98/98/792 dated 1-10-2012 and No. BR Dhaka 98/98/799 dated 2-10-2012, Annexures-1 and 1(1) respectively, both issued under the signature of Respondent No. 4 requesting Respondents No. 5 to 7 not to register any type of transfer/sale deed covering the properties in CS Plot No. 2497 and 2582 of CS Khatian No. 118 Mouza Baunia, JL No. 211 as found at page 510 of the "projabily property" Gazette (Annexure-C) which corresponds to SA Khatian Nos. 118/41, 118/76, 183, 184, 188, 198, 212, 220, 174, 179, 118/2 and 234 and also corresponds to RS Plot Nos. 6108, 6109, 6110, 6112 and 6116 of RS Khatian Nos. 63, 116, 117, 181, 240, 811, 818, 819, 862, 1083, 1371, 1490 and 1589, should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and of no legal effect, and/or pass such other or further order or, orders to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 3. Similarly, in Writ Petition No.17216 of 2012, Rule Nisi has been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned Memos, bearing No. BR Dhaka No. 98/98/792 dated 1-10-2012 and No. BR-Dhaka/98/98 / 799 dated 2-10-2012, Annexures J and J(1) respectively, both issued under the signature of Respondent No. 4 requesting Respondent Nos. 5 to 7 not to register any type of  4. Facts necessary for the disposal of Rule in Writ Petition No. 17056 of 2012, in short, are that the writ petitioners being involved in purchase and selling lands upon developing the same, intended to purchase 5.16 acre land of CS plot No. 2497 and 9.72 acre land of CS plot No. 2582, both of CS khatian No.118 of Mouza Baunia, under Police Station Pallabi, District-Dhaka, and accordingly contacted Md Ahsanullah and others, the SA, RS and Dhaka City Survey recorded owners, who are owning and possessing the same upon paying the land Development Taxes, in their names, to the government regularly. The said Writ petitioners, after being satisfied with the right, title and possession of the said owners in the aforesaid government records, took 9 registered powers of Attorney in their favour from the aforesaid owners in possession. But when the writ petitioners went to the respondent No. 6, the concerned sub-Registrar of Mirpur, for execution and registration of the deeds of sale by using those powers the said respondent refused to register the same on the plea that by the aforesaid two impugned Memoranda, being No. BR Dhaka-98/98/792, dated 1-10-212 and BR Dhaka-98/98/799 dated 2-10-2012 issued under the signature of respondent No.4, the present Manager, Court of Wards, Bhawal Raj Estate, under the management of the land Reform Board (Respondent No.3), he has been directed not to register any deed of transfer in respect of the said plots mentioned in the said two impugned memoranda. 

 5. On the other hand, the facts of the writ petition No. 17216 of 2012, in short, are that the writ petitioners, being a developer Company and its Managing Director, respectively, earlier purchased the properties contained in 17 CS Plots of Baunia Mouza, under Police Station Pallabi, from its lawful owners in possession, whose names have been duly successively recorded in the SA, RS and Dhaka City Survey khatians. Out of the aforesaid 17 CS plot 12 CS(plots being No. 2035, 2106, 2137, 2142, 2151, 2176, 2972, 2976, 2977, 2987, 3280, 3290 and 2977/3459, were commonly recorded under three CS Khatians being No. 554, 555 and 556 amongst which, two CS khatians, namely, 554 and 555 comprising of plot numbers 13, 285, 212, 3280, 2035, 2106, 3290, 2116, 3295, 2137, 2142, 2150, 2151, 2176, 2972, 2976, 2977, 2987, 3001, 3030, and 2977/3457 are recorded in the name of two private persons in the cadastral survey (CS) Khatian, who have had no connection, whatsoever, with the Court of Wards, Annexures B and B(1), respectively. The other CS khatian, being No. 556, was recorded in the name of the original owner, the then Zamindar, represented by the Court of Wards(Annexure-B-2). The remaining four CS plots, being No. 2748 and 2970 under CS khatian No. 118 and CS plot No. 3279 and No. 3280/3438 under CS khatian No. 12 and 646 respectively, were also recorded in the name of the original owner, the then Zamindar, represented by the Court of Wards in the CS record Annexure-C, C(1) and C(2) respectively, which were settled with the "projas" and, as such the said lands covering the aforesaid four khatians being "Projabily properties" the rent receiving interests thereof were acquired by the then government under the then government under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, by way of publishing "projabily property" gazette (Annexure-D) for which the rent received i.e. the Zamindar received compensations, as evident from Annexure-D(1). Pursuant to Annexure D and D (1) the Zamindars, as well as the Court of Wards, lost all right, title, interest and possession in those properties/plots by operation of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Consequently, all the subsequent record of rights, namely, the SA, RS and Dhaka City Survey. were duly prepared and finally published in the names of the previous projas upgrading them as owners and their subsequent successors and transferees as "owners' in possession whose title and possession are protected against all, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 as well as by the subsequent enactment of President's Order (PO) 90 of 1972. Under such circumstances, the writ petitioners, having purchased the said properties from the SA, RS and Dhaka City Survey recorded owners, went to respondent No. 6 for registration of the deeds of transfer of their purchased properties from those khatians to the subsequent transferees as well as also for registration of the deeds of purchase of other properties from the said plots but the said respondent, pursuant to the aforesaid two impugned Memoranda No. BR Dhaka-98/98/ 792, dated 1-10-2012 and BR Dhaka-98/98/799 dated 2-10-2012, Annexure-J and J(1), respectively, declined to register any transfer deed on the plea that respondent No. 4, Manager, Court of Wards, prohibited him from registering any deed connecting the aforesaid CS plots. 

 7. The Respondents Nos. 3 and 4 namely, the Land Reforms Board and the Court of Wards, entered appearance in both the Rules and filed affidavits in opposition contending inter alia that on the basis of recent decision and the directive of the Ministry of Land and also the Parliamentary Standing Committee for Ministry of Land, registration of any deed of transfer of any property belonging to the then Bhawal Raj Estate which are managed by the Court of Wards, has been stopped for the purpose of preserving the historic and heritage properties of the Bhawal Raj as such the said respondents have issued the impugned memos being duty bound to protect the interest of the Bhawal Raj. The said respondents in their affidavits did not deny the facts of acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the government. Rather in para 3 they also admitted the facts stated in the writ petitions stating to be matters of record. However, in para 10 they stated that the last record of right i.e. ''Dhaka City Survey;" was erroneously prepared and published in the name of illegal occupiers, which they did not establish by any paper. Having gone through the said affidavit-in-opposition, we could not understand the head and tail of the same. The affidavits in opposition filed in Writ Petition No.17056 of 2012 is not only chaotic but also Confusing. The respondents did not state as to how the property belongs to the court of wards or how the same are not "Projabily Properties" or how Annexure C and D to the aforesaid two writ petitions respectively, do not focus on the correct picture nor they could show that the court of wards took appropriate steps in last 60 years to protect the properties of the Bhawal Raj. Similar is the position in respect of the affidavit-in-opposition filed in Writ Petition No. 17216 of 2012. 

 8. Mr M Khalilur Rahman, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners in both the Rules, submits that when by operation of law the rent receiving interests of all the properties possessed by "projas", of all the seminaries vested with the government pursuant to sections 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and thereby raising the status of "projas" to those of "owners" of such lands and also declaring them to be the owners of the said land which they were settled with by the then Zamindars and accordingly, gazette notifications. (Annexure C in Writ Petition. No. 17056 of 2012 and Annexure D in Writ-petition No. 17216 of 2012) have been published incorporating the CS khatian numbers with mouzas, JL Numbers, thanas and, districts throughout the then East Pakistan, which were thereafter, by operation of law recorded in the names of the said "projas" transformed as "owners", the predecessors in interest of the petitioners, in the subsequent SA and RS records, giving them the title and accordingly, in the last Dhaka City Survey, the successors of such owners' name being recorded, the respondents have no right under any law to direct the registering authority not to register any document and as such, the embargo, as imposed by the impugned memos are not only illegal but also examples of high handedness. 

 9. He next submits that as it is known to everybody that in one khatian there may be several plot numbers and similar plot numbers may be available in different khatians citing ratio of shares of the owners, and in the impugned two memoranda no khatian number having been mentioned, the same are vague, indefinite and rather incomplete which cannot be applied on any land. In the absence of stating any khatian number in the impugned orders, rather simply upon incorporating only the CS plot numbers no specific right over any property can be construed, rather than to create confusion in the mind of the respondents No. 5 to 7, i.e. the registering authority as such the impugned orders are not sustainable under any law as the same are vague and indefinite. 

 11. On the other hand, Mr Faizul Kabir, along with Ms. Aysha Flora, the learned advocates appearing on behalf of Respondents No. 3 and 4, on the face of the submissions made by the learned advocates for the petitioners, in both the writ petitions, as to acquisition of the rent receiving interests of the Zamindars under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, could not make out any case in favour of the respondents. Mr Kabir did not put forward any argument on the publication of the "projabily property" gazette notification (Annexure-C in Writ Petition No. 17056 of 2012 and Annexure-D in Writ Petition No. 17216 of 2012) and also on finally published Dhaka City Survey in the names of the predecessor in interest of the petitioners. The learned advocate did not make any statement or submission on the presumptive value of the latest survey i.e. Dhaka City survey nor as to why no step has been taken for correcting the Dhaka City Survey, if any. Rather he simply confined himself within the submission that the property being historic and heritage property of Bhawal Raj, the respondents have taken appropriate steps to stop transferring such properties by the present petitioners, who are, according to him, mere "illegal occupants" and, as such, the impugned memos have been properly issued. Thus the writ petitions are not maintainable and both the Rules are liable to be discharged. 

 12. Heard the learned Advocates of both the parties, perused the two writ petitions, the affidavits in opposition and the Annexures appended to the two writ petitions. It appears that the properties of writ petition No. 17056 of 2012 bearing CS plot No. 2497 and 2582 have been recorded in CS Khatian No. 118 along with other CS plots. The said CS khatian No.118 appears at page 510 of the "projabily property" Gazette dated 24-3-1952 (Annexure-C) by which the rent receiving interest of the then Zamindars have been acquired by the government under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. It also appears that the previous Zamindar Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury has been paid up compensation for that purpose, as evident from compensation payment Gazette Notification No. 3126 dated 27-2-1956 published on 29-2-1956 in the then Dhaka Gazette, Annexure-C(1), by the then Government. Similarly, the properties of the writ petition No. 17216 of 2012, as it appears from Annexure B, B(1), B(2) and Annexures C, C (1) and C(2), that 43 CS plots in 6 Khatians out of which plots No. 2035, 2106, 2137, 2142, 2977, 2151, 2176, 2972, 2976, 2977, 2987, 3280, 3290 and 2977/3459 of CS Khatian 554 as well as those total khatian No. 555, total 26 plots, have been recorded in the names of private individuals, not the Zamindar or the court of wards. As such the court of wards has no connection, whatsoever, with the same. On the other hand 13 plots bearing same numbers namely, 2035, 2106, 2137, 2142, 2151, 2176, 2972, 2976, 2977, 2987, 3280, 3290 and 2977/3459 of CS Khatian No. 556 along with CS plots No.2748 and 2970 of CS khatian No.118 CS plot No.3280/3438 of CS Khatian No. 646 and CS plot No. 3279 of CS khatian No. 12 (total 17 plots) all were originally recorded in the name of the then Zamindar, Kumar Rabindra Narayan Ray Chowdhury, represented by the Court of Wards, the respondent No. 4, in the CS Survey, as appears from Annexure B, B(1), B(2), C,C(1) and C(2) respectively, which were settled with the. "projas" as underraiyts. Thereafter, with the enactment of the Statement Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the rent receiving interest the raiyots i.e. the then Zamindars vested with the government and the "projas" were upgraded and recognized by the government as owners of their settled land they had been possessing under the Zamindar. Under such circumstances in all subsequent surveys the previous "projas" and their successors names have been recorded as owners, duly recognized by the government. But it reveals that all the plots mentioned above in six khatians which have been recorded in the names of the then projas or their successors have been claimed as the properties of the Court of Wards without providing any khatian number by the impugned memos. On Examination of the "projabily property" Gazette it appears that the plots of CS khatian No. 556, 118, 646 and khatian No. 12 have been duly recorded as "projabily properties" whose "rent receiving" interests of the then Zamindars have been acquired by the government under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. As such whatever rights, title and interest, the Court of Wards, if any, had, in all these plots, have been ceased by the Government. In Annexure C to writ petition No. 17056 of 2012, the "Projabily Property" Gazette, at page 510 plots of CS khatian No. 118 have been enlisted as projabili properties. Similarly in Annexure-D to the writ petition No. 17216 of 2012 all the plots of CS khatians No.12, 118, 556 and 646 have been shown at pages 503, 510 and at page 516 respectively in the "projabily property" Gazette. 

 13. It further appears that following the "projabily property" Gazette the SA khatianswere published recording the names of the then "projas" upon upgrading their status as the "owners" in different SA khatians by the Survey and Settlement Department of the Government. Similarly, the next RS khatians were also prepared and published recording the names of the said "projas"/"owners" and their subsequent legal heirs and assignees as "owners". The Land Reform Board and the Court of wards as respondent No. 3 and 4, in both the writ petitions, respectively, did not deny the statements in respect of publishing the "projabily property" Gazette and the compensation payment Gazette and preparation and final publication of the SA and RS record of rights in the names of the previous "projas" and their successors in interests as "owners". Even in respect of preparation and publication of the recent Dhaka City Survey record the respondents frankly admitted, in paragraph-10 of their affidavit that those were recorded in the name of the previous "projas" as "owners" but claimed that those recordings as wrong although no step has yet been taken by the respondents to correct the said final recording, of course time allowed for correction of such wrong recording, as alleged, has expired long before. The learned Advocate for the petitioners referring to the "projabily property" Gazette (Annexure-C and D in the aforesaid two writ petitions, respectively) and also to the PO 90 of 1972 (Annexure-D and E in the aforesaid two writ petitions, respectively) and also to the decision of the Appellate Division in the case reported in 33 DLR (AD) /3 and 53, 27 DLR (SC) 109, and14 MLR (AD) 401 submitted that the Appellate Division in those cases has, already settled that the property mentioned in the "projabily property" Gazette are the properties of the projas and their successors in interests, as the rent receiving interest, therein, of the previous Zamindars have been acquired by the Government. As such when the petitioners went for registering the transfer deeds of the land purchased from the successor in interest of the then "projas", whose names 'have been correctly recorded and finally published in the aforesaid Khatians, the respondents No. 5 to 7' have no authority to refuse registration on the direction of respondents No. 3 and 4. Thus haying not done what they are suppose to do under the law they have committed illegality in not registering the deeds. 

 14. Under such circumstances, when the said plots are published, in the gazette notification as "Projabily Properties" and the rent receiving interests of the then Zamindars are acquired under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (hereafter referred to as the SAT Act) the same no longer belongs to the then Zamindars or the Court of Wards rather to the "projas" as per SAT Act 1950 who have been upgraded and declared to be the "owners", the respondents have no authority to issue the impugned notices. Moreover when no khatian number has been mentioned, in the impugned memos simply mentioning the CS plot, numbers does not specify the land as such, the impugned notices are vague and indefinite by which no legal force can be ascertained. Section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, reads as follows: 

 16. The Appellate Division in the case of People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Sri Sri Madan Gopal Jew Bigraha , reported in 33 DLR (AD) 13 after considering and discussing the legal effect of the aforesaid laws, held that 'with the publication of notifications under section 3 all rent-receiving interests including wakf and debuttor property stood acquired by and vested in the Government'. Again in the ease of Promode Ranjan Saha and others vs Government of Bangladesh and another, reported in 33 DLR (AD) 53 it has been observed that 'after the promulgation of PO 90 of 72 all orders including orders of injunction, etc. passed in appeals, application, etc. shall cease to have any effect and no court shall entertain any fresh suit, appeal, application, etc. in which the legality of any such law of acquisition is challenged or called in question'. In the case of Anwara Begum Chowdhurani vs Nur Jahan Begum reported in 27 DLR (AD) 109 it has been held that 'after the notification issued under section 3 of the Act the status of the under-raiyat became upgraded to that of raiyat. The rent receiving interests can be acquired even before the preparation of record of rights and publication of compensation assessment rolls'. It has further been held therein that 'with the acquisition of the rent-receiving interests by the government all intermediary interests disappeared and a person holding the land under the government becomes a "tenant", becomes a "raiyat" or a "Malik" of the land recognized by the government. Consequently, the under-raiyat who actually holds the land becomes a tenant under the government. Superior land lord (i.e. the raiyat) of an under-raiyat by virtue of elimination of his rent-receiving interests disappears and the under-raiyat is upgraded to the status of a "raiyat". Lastly, in the case of Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate vs Rasheda Begum and others reported in 14 MLR (AD) 401 the Appellate Division has held " record of rights prepared and finally published under section 144 cannot be varied by any authority and remedy of wrong entry if any lies with the appropriate court'. It has further been held in that judgment by the Appellate Division that "Manager, Bhawal Raj estate, Court of Wards can manage only the retainable land." The Appellate Division in the aforesaid cases has already settled that the property enlisted/ shown in the "projabily property" Gazette are the properties of "projas" who have been accepted as "owners" and the "rent receiving" interest whatsoever it had therein, of the Zamindars all vested to the Government by operation of SAT Act, 1950. The relevant portion of the finding of the Appellate Division in the case reported in 14 MLR (AD) 401 are as follows: 

 "The learned advocate appearing for the leave petitioner, when confronted with the aforesaid gazette notifications dated 24-3-1952 and 29-2-956, as to acquisition of rent receiving interest and the vesting of lands of the leave petitioners, including the case lands, found it difficult to substantiate the locus-standi of the leave petitioner in challenging the draft records of right prepared in the names of the respective writ petitioners in respect of their respective case lands prepared during the Mohanagar Survey. Further with the publication of the gazette notifications dated 24-3-1952 and 29-2-1956 the leave petitioner ceased to have any right, title and interest and possession in the case lands, because of acquisition, and vesting of said lands in the Government. "Thereafter, the full bench of the Hon'ble Appellate Division, on an application corrected the said judgment stating that the rent receiving interest of Projabily Property had vested to the Government and land has been vested to the projas as owners. In that case the Court of Wards, Bhawal Raj Estate and the Land Reform Board the present contesting respondents were parties and had challenged the Dhaka City Survey khatian prepared and published in the names of the successors in interests of the projas". The Apex Court in that case further held: 

 "Thus we are of the view that the leave petitioner had no locus-standi to challenge the draft Mohanagar Survey khatian as prepared in the names of the respective writ petitioners, at-least after publication of the gazette notifications dated 24-3-1952 and 29-2-1956." 

 19. Considering the provisions of law mentioned above and the findings of the Appellate Division in the aforesaid cited cases we are of the view that the property in question in both the Rules being "Projabily properties", as evident from Annexures C and D to Writ Petition No. 17056 of 2012 and Writ Petition No. 17216 of 2012, respectively, and the same being finally published in SA, RS and Dhaka Mohanagar City Survey khatians in the name of the predecessors in interest of the petitioners and the then Zamindars having not taken any step in respect of wrong entry, as claimed by the respondents, the court of wards, the said respondents cannot, under any circumstance, claim that the property belongs to the court of wards. As such when the property does not belong to the court of wards the court of wards has no legal authority to direct the registering authority not to register any deed of transfer in respect of the said properties. 

 22. Apart from the above, we want to focus about the role of the learned advocate for the respondents as well as the respondents No. 3 and 4. We find it very difficult to understand from the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the Respondents No. 3 and 4 that what is the gist of the case of the respondents and the respondents without stating the fact that the respondents are the owners of the land and, as such, have issued such directions upon the registering authority rather stated that the impugned memos have been issued for protecting the historic and heritage properties of Bhawal Raj. Nor the respondents could show that the registering authority has responsibility to abide by such directions and thereby refusal to registration has been done in accordance with law. On the other hand, respondents No. 3 and 4 could not come forward with any piece of document to show that they have right, title or possession in the land in question, specifically, when the property has been published in the gazette notification under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the said publication being finalized and protected by PO 90 of 1972, the respondents No. 3 and 4 did not come for-ward to assist the court by showing a piece of paper for the said plots, which have already been recorded in the name of the projas fall within the "retainable khas land" of the Zamindars being up to 375 bighas with the commencement of the SAT Act, 1950 which has subsequently been reduced to 100 Bigas and lastly to 60 bighas. The respondents No. 3 and 4 did not even come forward with any piece of paper to show that the limit of retainable khas land has been raised to more than 60 bighas for which the court of wards can act as the custodian. 

 25. Before withdrawing our pen, we would like to note that, now a days time and again we are confronted with unnecessary and uncalled for litigations like the present one in spite of settling the selfsame issue connecting with "projabily property" by the Apex court in its different decisions reported in, 33 DLR (AD) 13 and 53, 27 DLR (SC) 109 and lastly in the case reported in 14 MLR (AD) 401. In these two writ petitions the question over the title of "projabily property" of the previous Zamindar, Kumar Rabindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury, represented by the Court of Wards, Bhawal Raj Estate, again came up for our consideration as the court of Wards claimed the "projabily property" as its own property and accordingly issued the two "impugned Memoranda, though it has already been settled earlier in the aforesaid cases holding that the "projabily properly" can never be claimed by the previous Zamindars represented by the court of Wards. The Court of Wards though legally bound to follow the said decision according to Article 112 of the constitution but time and again they are harassing the people claiming title over the "projabily property", either by issuing Memorandum or by other ways and means and thereby also wasting the courts valuable time. So it is high time to caution the Court of Wards, Bhawal Raj Estate and also the Land Reform Board to abstain from creating such situation on frivolous issues and thereby pushing the public to the Court. Thus they are cautioned not to harass anybody specifically the previous "projas" or their successors-in-interests any more, claiming title over the "projabily property" as cited in the "projabily property" gazette published on 24-3-1952. If in future, any such illegal and uncalled for claim is sought for by the court of wards or if any litigation is continuing or started afresh because of court of wards action by claiming title over the said "projabily property" by the Court of Wards and the Land Reform Board, then they would be liable to be dealt with for contempt of Court, apart from such litigations been abated under PO 90 of 1972.

2. Predecessor of the plaintiffs, late Moulvi Joynal Abedin purchased the suit land in revenue sale held on 11 July 1942. The judgment debtor namely, Haralal challenged the sale by filing Title Suit No. 48 of 1942 but lost it at all stages and finally in second appeal which was dismissed on 3 August 1948. Joynal Abedin mutated his name and paid rent all through till his death in 1960 and his name was recorded in the preliminary Record-of-rights. But after his death the heirs of his brother Dr. Abdul Halim in collusion with Revenue Officers got their names recorded in the finally published khatian in respect of 8 annas share of the suit land, putting up the claim that the revenue sale was benami transaction in that Dr. Abdul Halim younger brother of Joynal Abedin, had purchased 8 annas share in the land and that there was threat of dispossession of the plaintiffs from half of the land. Hence the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 502 of 1975. 

 3. Defendant respondents contested the suit denying the allegations and claiming that Joynal Abedin admitted the joint purchase and relinquished his claim to the extent of 8 annas share by a registered Nadabipatra dated 21 June, 1945 in the basis of which the finally published khatian recorded their 8 annas inter-est. The suit was decreed by the trial court. Both the trial court and the lower appellate court concurrently found that the Nadabipatra was forged document, copy of which was produced for the first time after the death of Joynal Abedin, that the finally published khatian in favour of joint purchase got no basis and on those findings decreed the suit. In second appeal S.A. No. 375 of 1979 a learned Single Ridge of the High Court Division observed that the concurrent findings were not sustainable in law as the courts below wrongly shifted the onus of proof of the benami purchase and the Nadabipatra upon the defendants.

2. Predecessor of the plaintiffs, late Moulvi Joynal Abedin purchased the suit land in revenue sale held on 11 July 1942. The judgment debtor namely, Haralal challenged the sale by filing Title Suit No. 48 of 1942 but lost it at all stages and finally in second appeal which was dismissed on 3 August 1948. Joynal Abedin mutated his name and paid rent all through till his death in 1960 and his name was recorded in the preliminary Record-of-rights. But after his death the heirs of his brother Dr. Abdul Halim in collusion with Revenue Officers got their names recorded in the finally published khatian in respect of 8 annas share of the suit land, putting up the claim that the revenue sale was benami transaction in that Dr. Abdul Halim younger brother of Joynal Abedin, had purchased 8 annas share in the land and that there was threat of dispossession of the plaintiffs from half of the land. Hence the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 502 of 1975. 

 3. Defendant respondents contested the suit denying the allegations and claiming that Joynal Abedin admitted the joint purchase and relinquished his claim to the extent of 8 annas share by a registered Nadabipatra dated 21 June, 1945 in the basis of which the finally published khatian recorded their 8 annas inter-est. The suit was decreed by the trial court. Both the trial court and the lower appellate court concurrently found that the Nadabipatra was forged document, copy of which was produced for the first time after the death of Joynal Abedin, that the finally published khatian in favour of joint purchase got no basis and on those findings decreed the suit. In second appeal - S.A. No. 375 of 1979 a learned Single Ridge of the High Court Division observed that the concurrent findings were not sustainable in law as the courts below wrongly shifted the onus of proof of the benami purchase and the Nadabipatra upon the defendants.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Syed J.R. Mudassir Hussain

lawyer:
Julfiquir Bulbul Chowdhury with Md. Shariful Islam, Advocates— For the Petitioners. 
Md. Ekramul Islam, Advocate—For Opposite party Nos. 1-13.
parties:
Younus Sonar alias Younus Ali Sonar and others ------- Petitioners
vs
Abdul Samad and others ------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
3. Facts, relevant for the purpose of disposal of this Rule, are that Ismail Sonar, the predecessor of opposite party Nos. 1-13, as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 155 of 1922 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Rajshahi against Gulzar Ali Sonar and others in which the present petitioner was defendant No. 34 praying for a decree of partition of 0.89 acre land claiming eight anna four gonda share upon deducting 0.07 acre land there from. The suit was transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Charghat, Rajshahi and renumbered as Other Suit No. 46 of 1990. The case of the plaintiff is that 0.89 acre land as described in the schedule to the plaint belonged to Emran Sonar in eight anna share, Jarimon Bibi in three anna four gonda share, Sabjan Bewa in sixteen gonda share and Kamani Bewa in four anna share and accordingly, CS Khatian No. 220 was prepared and finally published in their name. Sabjan Bewa died leaving behind one daughter Jamiron Bibi and husband Emran Sonar. Jamiron Bibi died leaving behind three sons Koshimuddin Sonar. Abdul Hamid, Abdul Kader and four daughters Sokina, Hamidon, Samina and Maleka (defendant No. 30). Abdul Kader died leaving behind five sons (defendant Nos. 12-16). one daughter (defendant No. 17) and one wife (defendant No. 18) as his heirs. Abdul Hamid died leaving behind three sons (defendant Nos. 8-10) and one daughter (defendant No. 11). Kashimuddin Sonar died leaving behind three sons (defendant Nos. 1-3), three daughters (defendant Nos. 4-6) and one wife (defendant No. 7). Hamidon died leaving behind two sons (defendant Nos. 22-23), one daughter (defendant No. 24) and husband (defendant No. 23). Sokina died leaving behind one son (defendant No. 19) and two daughters (defendant Nos. 20-21). Samina died leaving behind husband (defendant No. 25), one son (defendant No. 26) and two daughters (defendant No. 27-28). Kamani Bewa died leaving behind one son Abdus Shukur, who died leaving behind two daughters (defendant Nos. 31-32) and one wife (defendant No. 33). Thereafter, Emran Sonar died leaving behind one son, the plaintiff. In the aforesaid way the plaintiff inherited eight anna and four gonda share out of 0.89 acre suit land. The plaintiff has got his ancestral homestead in Plot No. 1912 and out of his share he sold 0.07 acre land of Plot No. 1873 to Sairuddin long ago who got his joma separated from the original jote by mutation and, as such, he was not impleaded in this suit. Said 0.07 acre land would be deducted from the share of the plaintiff. 

 6. Out of the defendants, only defendant No. 34 contested the suit by filing written statements contending that the suit was not maintainable, barred by limitation and there was no community of interest between the parties for partition of the suit property. The positive case of the defendant was that the CS recorded tenants voluntarily surrendered their rayoti right to the superior landlords from whom Bashanto Kumar took pattan and paid rent to the landlords. The plaintiff took settlement of 0.23 acre land from the suit jote from Bashanto Kumar and erected dwelling house therein and thereafter, SA Khatian No. 157 and RS Khatian No. 134 were prepared and finally published in his name. Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land out of the suit property along with other land measuring total 2.305 acre by registered sale deed No. 7799 dated 9-5-1952 to Younus Sonar (defendant No. 34). While Younus Sonar was owning and possessing said 0.59 acre land from the suit jote separate SA Khatian No. 155 and RS Khatian No. 117 were prepared and finally published in his name. The plaintiff has no right, title to or interest in 0.59 acre land and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 2. Though CS record was prepared and finally published in one Khatian but during SA and RS operation the land of CS Khatian was separated and three separate SA Khatians and three separate RS Khatians have been prepared and finally published out of which one SA Khatian and its corresponding RS khatian have been prepared and finally published in the name of defendant No. 34 and two other separate SA Khatians and its two separate RS Khatinas have been prepared and finally published in the name of the plaintiff and, as such, the plaintiff is not a co-sharer of defendant No. 34. Moreover, in the plaint the plaintiff himself stated that defendant No. 34 was not a co-sharer in the suit holding. 

 6. Defendant No. 34 purchased 0.59 acre land including 0.26 acre land from Bashanto Kumar by registered sale deed dated 9-10-1952 following which separate SA and RS Khatians have been prepared and finally published in his name and he has been paying rents to the jaminders and thereafter, to the Government and has been possessing 0.59 acre land continually and uninterestedly from 1952 and, as such, defendant No. 34 acquired title therein by adverse possession and the right, title or interest, if any, of the CS recorded tenants have been extinguished and the plaintiff could not acquire title through CS recorded tenants. 

 4. Since 0.54 acre land of CS and SA Plot No. 1912 corresponding to RS Plot No. 4003 has not partitioned by metes and bounds, publication of said land in separate SA and RS Khatians in the name of plaintiff and defendant No. 34 did not cease their co-sharership and, as such, the par ties have community of interest in the suit property and the suit is maintainable. 

 12. Apart from adducing three oral witnesses the plaintiff produced CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1), the application of Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1970 (Exhibit-2), the judgment and order passed in the pre-emption case (Exhibit-3), certified copy of RS Khatian Nos. 117, 133 and 134 (Exhibits-4 series) and SA Khatian Nos. 156 and 157 (Exhibits-5 series). On the other hand, defendant No. 34 adduced three oral witnesses and also produced Jamindary rent receipt (Exhibit-Ka), the rent receipt showing payment of rent by Emran Sonar to Bashanto Kumar (Exhibit-Kha series), rent receipts showing payment of rent by Ismail Sonar (Exhibit-Ga series), one pattani receipt (Exhibit-Gha), twelve rent receipts showing payment of rent to the Government (Exhibit-Uma series), the original sale deed No. 7799 dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit-Cha), certified copy of SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Chha), certified copy of RS Khatian No. 117 (Exhibit-Ja), order passed in a proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and application filed therein (Exhibits-Jha and Neo). 

 13. Admittedly, 0.89 acre land appertaining to 0.07 acre of CS Plot No. 1873, 0.28 acre of CS Plot No. 1911 and 0.54 acre of CS Plot No. 1912 belonged to the father of the plaintiff in eight anna share and three others in eight anna share as CS Khatian was duly published in their name which has been proved by certified copy of CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1). The plaintiff claimed eight anna four gonda share after deducting 0.07 acre land out of total 0.89 acre land of CS Khatian No. 220. His case is that his father Emran Sonar had eight anna share in the suit land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1) and he also inherited four gonda share from his wife Sobjan Bewa and after his death the plaintiff inherited eight anna and four gonda share from the suit jote. The plaintiff also claimed title to 0.26 acre land on the basis of judgment dated 27-6-1979 passed in Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1970 and to prove the judgment, he produced its certified copy (Exhibit-3). On the contrary, defendant No. 34 contended that the CS recorded tenants voluntarily surrendered their raiyoti right to the superior landlords and after surrender, Bashanto Kumar took settlement and paid rent to the landlords and thereafter, Ismail Sonar (the plaintiff) took settlement of 0.23 acre land from Bashanto Kumar and constructed dwelling house therein and thereafter, SA Khatian No. 157 [Exhibit-5 (Ka)] and its corresponding RS Khatian No. 134 [Exhibit-4(Kha)] were prepared and finally published in his name. His further contention is that Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land along with other land to him by registered sale deed No. 7799 dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit-Cha) and thereafter, separate SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Cha) and its corresponding RS Khatian No. 117 [Exhibit-Ja (4)] have been prepared and finally published in his name and he has been owning and possessing the same uninterruptedly, on payment of rent for more than 12 years. 

 15. PW2 Abdus Sattar, deposed in support of the case of the plaintiff, stated in his cross-examination that the plaintiff possesses 14/15 decimal land. Upon Evaluation of the evidence of the PWs, the trial Court held that the PWs could not prove the case of the plaintiff rather, they deposed adversely to the plaintiff and admitted that defendant No. 34 had possession in the suit land and that the plaintiff could not adduce any evidence to show that defendant No. 34 was a permissive possessor under the plaintiff or his predecessor. The trial Court finally came to conclusion that the plaintiff could not prove his claim. However, the trial Court found title to and possession in 0.23 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 in favour of the plaintiff as per admission of the defendant No. 34. The Court of appeal, it appears that, did not discuss oral or documentary evidence of the parties independently but concurred with the findings of the trial Court. The plaintiff did not challenge the adverse findings of the Courts below by preferring any appeal before higher forum. Accordingly, it is to be presumed that he accepted the findings and decision of the courts below that he acquired title to 0.23 acre land as per admission of defendant No. 34 and that the CS recorded tenants including the father of the plaintiff surrendered tenancy right to the superior landlords from whom Bashanto Kumar took settlement afresh and then settled 0.23 acre land to the plaintiff and on the basis of such settlement SA Khatian No. 157 and its corresponding RS Khatian No. 134 were rightly prepared and finally published in the name of the plaintiff in respect of 0.23 acre land and that the plaintiff could not prove permissive possession of defendant No. 34. 

 17. Now question arises as to whether the plaintiff is entitled to 0.26 acre land in view of the judgment passed in pre-emption case. The plaintiff produced certified copy of judgment of the pre-emption case, marked as Exhibit-3, from which it reveals that the plaintiff of present suit as petitioner filed the pre-emption case to enforce the right of pre-emption of 0.26 acre land purported to be sold by opposite party Nos. 7-16 of that case (who were the heirs of CS recorded tenants) vide sale deed dated 3-9-1969 in favour of the sons of defendant No. 34. On the other hand, opposite party Nos. 1-6 and 31 (present defendant No. 34) and 38, 39 contested the pre-emption case by filing three separate written objections. In that pre-emption case opposite party Nos. 1-6 and 31 contended that they never purchased 0.26 acre land from opposite party Nos. 7-16 and the disputed deed dated 3-9-1969 was collusive and without any consideration. Defendant No. 34 of this suit contended in that pre-emption case that he purchased 0.59 acre land including 0.26 acre land along with other lands in 1952 and he was owning and possessing the same and the petitioner of the pre-emption case was not a co-sharer of the disputed holding and opposite party Nos. 7-16 had no saleable interest in 0.26 acre land. Both parties adduced evidence in that case and upon considering the evidence, the trial Court held that there was a sale in respect of said 0.26 acre land and the pre-emptor (the plaintiff) was a co-sharer to the disputed land and finally observed and gave verdict as follows: 

 19. In this case, it appears that the trial Court after evaluating rent receipts (Exhibits-Kha series and Uma series) and original sale deed dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit Cha) as well as SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Chha) and RS Khatian No. 117 (Exhibit-Ja) observed that after purchase in 1952 defendant No. 34 has been paying rents of the suit land to the jaminders and thereafter, to the Government. But without giving any finding in regards acquisition of title to 0.59 acre land by defendant No. 34, the trial Court erroneously held that the plaintiff would get saham of 0.26 acre land from CS Plot No. 1911 as per judgment of Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 1970. The Court of appeal committed the same error and illegally allotted 0.26 acre land. 

 21. As mentioned earlier, the trial Court after evaluating rent receipts (Exhibits-Kha series and Uma series) and original sale deed dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit Cha) as well as SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Chha) and RS Khatian No. 117 (Exhibit-Ja) produced by defendant No. 34 observed that after purchase in 1952 defendant No. 34 has been paying rents of the suit land to the jaminders and thereafter, to the Government which has been upheld by the Court of appeal. Defendant No. 34 produced original sale deed dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit-Cha) from which it appears that Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land and rent receiving interest of 0.23 acre land to defendant No. 34. This sale deed dated 9-10-1952 is more or less admitted by the plaintiff in the way that Bashanto Kumar had no saleable interest to transfer said 0.59 acre land to defendant No. 34 because he was a permissive possessor under the plaintiff. But both the Courts below as well as the Court who passed judgment in the pre-emption case found that the plaintiff or the petitioner in the pre-emption case could not prove the fact of permissive possession. Moreover, sale deed dated 9-10-1952 was attained 30 years of age at the date when it was tendered to evidence on 23-9-1997, original "of which was produced from proper custody and, as such, as per section 90 of the Evidence Act it is to be presumed as genuine document and that the signature and every other part of the document is genuine. As per section 92 of the Evidence Act oral or extraneous evidence to contradict the terms of contents of a document is inadmissible. However, the plaintiff did not adduce any oral or documentary evidence to prove that Exhibit-Cha was a product of forgery. As per recital of sale deed dated 9-10-1952, Bashanto Kumar was a tenant of 0.28 acre land of CS Plot No. 1911 and 0.54 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 under Putia Jaminder of Rajshahi. The plaintiff was under-tenant from Bashanto Kumar in respect of 0.23 acre land out of 0.54 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 and Bashanto Kumar transferred entire land of his khas possession and rent receiving interest of 0.23 acre land to defendant No. 34 and handed over possession of 0.28 acre land of CS Plot No. 1911 and 0.31 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 in favour of defendant No. 34. Since sale deed dated 9-10-1952 is an old document of avove 30 years, as per section 90 read with section 91 of the Evidence Act, the recital of the deed dated 9-10-1952 are presumed to be correct. Moreover, during SA operation said 0.59 acre land was recorded in the name of defendant No. 34 in SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit Cha) and 0.23 acre land was recorded in the name of the plaintiff in separate SA Khatian No. 157 (Exhibit-5 Ka) and thereafter, their corresponding RS Khatian No. 117 ( Exhibit-Ja) in respect of 0.59 acre land was prepared and finally published in the name of defendant No. 34 and RS Khatian No. 134 [Exhibit-4 (Kha)] in respect of 0.23 acre land was prepared and finally published in the name of the plaintiff. Moreover, the courts below found that defendant No. 34 paid rent to the Jaminder and Government. The above facts lead to irresistible presumption that the sale deed dated 9-10-1952 has been acted upon. The plaintiff could not produce any evidence to discard the such presumption. 

 22. Considering the evidences of the parties, it is evident that though total 0.89 acre land was recorded in CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1) in the name of Emran Sonar, the father of the plaintiff and others, as tenant under superior landlords but subsequently, Bashanto Kumar became tenant of 0.89 acre land under the superior landlords out of which he settled 0.23 acre land to the plaintiff and thus the plaintiff became under-tenant under Basanto Kumar and then Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land under his khas possession along with rent receiving interest of 0.23 acre land to defendant No. 34 following which separate SA and RS khatians were prepared and finally published in their respective names and defendant No. 34 acquired title to 0.59 acre land and the plaintiff acquired title to 0.23 acre land. 

 24. The suit property is an agricultural land and that the defendant No. 34 is a stranger purchaser to the suit holdings and the tenancy of CS Khatian in respect of the suit holdings has been separated by preparation and publication of three sets of separate SA and RS Khatians in the name of the plaintiff and defendant No. 34. Accordingly, the plaintiff and defendant No. 34 are not co-sharers of the suit holdings. Moreover, in one part of the plaint, the plaintiff asserted that he has no community of interest with defendant No. 34 and in other part, he stated that cause of action of the suit arose in the event of pronouncement of judgment in the pre-emption case. Accordingly, the plea of the plaintiff is self contradictory leading to no cause of action for filing this suit. In view of the above, question of community of interest between the parties does not arise at all and the present suit for recovery of khas possession in the guise of suit for partition is not maintainable.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No.8 of 1979.
lawyer:
MihirKanti Majumder with Hemayet Hossain, Jatirmoya Deb for Jitendra Narayan Deb, Advocates ----- For the Appellants,
BK Das, Advocate ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Madaris Ali and others ----- Appellants
Vs
Biswamber Das Being dead his heirs ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
5. Contesting defendant Nos. 1 to 8, 10 and 13 denied the material allegations made in the plaint. They further averred that the plaintiffs suit is not maintainable and barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Their specific case is that Syedunnessa Chowdhurani, Khan Bahadur Gousuddin Ahmed Chowdhury and others did never settle the suit land 40 years ago or at any time with the plaintiffs at an annual rental of half a maund of paddy per kedar or any rent nor they realised any rent from them. Suit land was Khas dakhali land of the said landlords and the same was fallow land even during the land settlement operation and recorded as such in the name of the proforma defendants in the khatians. In 1380 BS principal defendants entered into an agreement with the proforma defendants to purchase the suit land at the rate of Tk. 1250.00 per acre and with the permission of the said owners principal defendant Nos. 14 to 19 sold 24 acre of the suit land in their 14 annas 12 gondas 35 tils share at a consideration of Tk. 30,000 to the principal defendants by a registered sale deed dated 22nd Falgoon, 1381 BS (27.3.75) and the said sellers relinquished all their right, title and interest in the said land in favour of defendants 1 to 13 and the principal defendants have been possessing the same along with 1 anna 7 gondas 3 koras 5 tils shares of proforma defendants 20 and 21 who could not execute and register the sale deed for some difficulties but made over possession of the same to the defendants 1 to 13. Plaintiffs failed to purchase the suit land as the principal defendants offered more money than they had offered and they filed the suit on false allegation of settlement. They had never any title and possession in the suit land. 

 6. Plaintiffs examined 6 witnesses including plaintiff No. 3 Mobarak Ali as PW 1 and also produced and proved some Toka Farags Exts. 1 to 1 (r) in support of their case. Contesting defendants examined 5 witnesses including defendant No. 7 Rowab Ali as DW 1 and also produced and proved some documents such as finally published Khatians Ext. A (2), the government rent receipts Ext. B to B(2) and certified copy of their kabala Ext. C. 

 "In spite of all the defects in" the Toka farags it has now become clear that the plaintiffs have their legs on the suit land and whatever defects crept in the Toka farags have since been perfected by the long user of the suit land by the plaintiffs beyond the statutory period of limitation to the knowledge of the original owners. Khatian Ext A is found to be erroneous and kabala Ext. C is found to have no legal effect. As the plaintiffs have clear title and possession in the suit land the suit is found to be maintainable in the present form." 

 8. Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder along with Mr. Hemayet Hossain and Mr. Jotirmoya Deb. learned Advocates, appearing on behalf of Mr. Jitendra Narayan Deb for the appellants, placed before us plaint, written statement, deposition of the witnesses, impugned judgment and other materials on record. The learned Advocate submitted that the plaintiffs failed to establish their alleged claim of settlement of the suit land on the basis of Toka farags Ext. 1 series which are neither in the name of any of the plaintiffs nor any particulars of the suit land mentioned therein. He further submitted that the plaintiffs also failed to establish their alleged adverse possession beyond the statutory period of limitation. He further submitted that the suit land was recorded in the name of predecessor-in-interest of the proforma defendants in finally published Khatians after factual field survey in the locality and the suit land has been recorded as fallow land (layek-patiti/ Layek ura). 

 10. In this case admittedly the suit land belonged to the predecessors-in-interest of the proforma defendants and it was their vacant Khas land and finally published khatians Ext. A series recorded the same in the name of the said landlords as their Khas land. The question in whether the said landlords settled the same with the plaintiffs and or the plaintiffs acquired title therein by adverse possession. 

 13. There is no case of the plaintiffs that they entered into the suit lands forcibly at any point of time to the knowledge of the said landlords, who admittedly reside far away and who has no tahsil office in the locality, denying title of the said landlords. Admittedly suit land was recorded in the name of the landlords Sayedunnessa Chowdhurani and Khan Bahadur Gousuddin Ahmed Chowdhury and others in Khatian Nos. 16 and 112 of mouza Purnakhola and Khatian No. 581 of Mouza Chaluia Exts. A-(2) and the said land has been recorded as fallow land in khas possessions of the said persons. It is admitted by the learned Advocates of both the parties that at the time of acquisition of rent receiving interest under the SAT Act field survey operation for preparation of record of rights under the provisions of Sylhet Tenancy Act 1936 in the suit locality was going on and ultimately the record of rights were prepared and finally published under the provisions of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as there was no previous settlement operation in the District of Sylhet. Relying on the evidence of PW 1 the learned Advocate for the respondents contended that the said Khatians were wrongly prepared in the name of the landlords. PW 1 in his deposition stated that during last settlement operation they entrusted Morals and Karmacharies of landlords to record the suit land in their name. But in cross-examination he admitted that he has other lands besides the suit land and those were correctly recorded in his name. We have already seen that there was no tahsil office of the Zamindars in the locality and as such entrusting Karmacharies of the Zamindars cannot be relied on. None has corroborated the PW 1 in this respect and he also failed to name the Moral or Karmachari whom the plaintiffs had entrusted for the purpose. Moreover, the plaintiffs never took care to enquire about the Khatians within the period of 12 years from the date of final publication of the Khatians in 1963 and they only enquired about the Khatians in 1975 when they came to know from the principal defendants about the sale of the suit land by the proforma defendants to the principal defendants. The plaintiffs neither claimed to have paid any rent to the Government from 1363 BS till the time of filing the suit in 1382 BS nor produced and proved any rent receipts. In view of the above it is difficult to hold that the said Khatians were not correctly prepared in the name of said Zamindars. Such finally published SA Khatians prepared after field survey operation stand on much better footing and more reliable than the SA Khatians made by merely revising the CS Khatians. 

 15. From the above discussion, it is clear that the plaintiffs' failed to prove their possession in the suit land Plaintiffs claim that they made the suit land fit for cultivation 40 years ago after taking settlement and grew paddy therein is also belied by the entry in the khatians Ext. A series classifying the suit lands as Layak patit layck/ura i.e. follow land in Khas possession of the predecessor of the proforma defendants. It is well settled that possession follows title. Even occasional surreptitious acts of possession on the part of the plaintiffs behind the back of such recorded owners who were admittedly residents of a distant place in the absence of any evidence of forcible entry in the land in denial of title of such owners cannot amount to adverse possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. 

 16. Court below did not assign any reason for finding the khatians Ext. A series to be erroneous and kabala Ext. C to have no legal effect, admittedly Syedunnessa Chowdhurani and others were the owners of the suit land and proforma defendants 14 to 21 as their heirs inherited the same. As the plaintiffs failed to establish their settlement of the same from the said landlords we find no reason how the court below could hold the said khatians in the names of the said landlords to be erroneous and the kabala in favour of the principal defendants to have no legal effect. Had the plaintiffs acquired any title in the suit land they would have paid rent for the same to the Government from 1363 BS after the acquisition of rent receiving interest. They utterly failed to make out any such case of payment of rent to the Government. How could the plaintiffs enjoy the suit land from 1363 BS till the time of filing the suit as claimed by them without paying rent to the Government? Any lay cultivator is quite conscious that he cannot enjoy the land without paying rent to the Government. Had the plaintiffs acquired any interest or title in the suit land they would have endeavored to pay rent to the Government and would have taken steps at the earliest opportunity to get the Khatians corrected in their names. But they have been sitting idle and now have arisen from their deep slumber after lapse of such a long time when the principal defendants purchased the suit land from the proforma defendants. On the other hand, we find from Ext. B series that the contesting defendants paid rents for the years 1379-82 BS vide Ext. B series. These go to show that all previous rents were paid by the recorded owners of the said land as stated by the DW 1 in cross-examination.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 30 of 2005
lawyer:
Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on-record ----- For the Petitioners 
Respondents ----- Not represented
parties:
Yusuf Ali and another ----- Petitioners
VS
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the D.C. Sylhet and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
3. The suit was filed seeking declaration of title, confirmation of possession and for a decree of permanent injunction. It was averred in the plaint that the land in suit since petty settlement is known as Bhut Bhuti Nala and Jur Beel and was recorded in C.S. patta No. 89, that during R.S. operation the said land was recorded in the name of Loke Patni and Others as Mahal Shamil Jalkar in patta No 5, that plaintiff Nos. 1-6's predecessor Syed Alim purchased 14 annas share of the land in suit in 1955 and the rest 2 annas share was purchased by plaintiff No. 7, that although at the initial stage of survey the khatian was prepared in the name of Loke Patni and others but in the finally published khatian names of some other persons were also recorded along with the name of Loke Patni and others, that the land in suit gradually silted up and lost its original character i.e. nala and beel and thereby became fit for boro cultivation, that Loke Patni excavated a 'Khal' over the suit land for irrigation purpose and same has been recorded in Dag No. 18, that the land in suit is partly boro land and there is Government khas land by the side of the land in suit and the same has been settled with the cultivators for boro cultivation, that defendant Nos. 1-4 have been contemplating to settle the land in suit to defendant No.5, hence the Suit seeking the relief for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and for permanent injunction. 

 5. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record held that Ext.5 khatian shows that Loke Patni and others possessed the land in suit for use on behalf of their co-villagers and the same is Jalkar, that Ext.2 patta and Ext.5 khatian shows that only Jalkar was leased out and Exts.6 and 6(a) show that the land in suit is marshy land and thus from the said documents it is seen that the land in suit is beel land and in all probability in the fringe of the Jalkar fishery boro is cultivated, that the land in suit is not the boro land but Jalkar, that Loke Patni and others did not acquire any saleable interest in the land in suit and they had only jalker right in suit, as evidenced by Ext. c, record has been prepared in the name of the Government, that no material has been brought on record to show that after purchase in 1955 plaintiffs paid rent, that no explanation has been offered for not producing the original kabalas on the basis whereof plaintiffs are claiming the land in suit, that there is no averment in the plaint as to why the plaintiffs are not in possession of the kabalas by which they have purchased the land in suit, that at the time of trial attempt was made through the deposition of P.W.2 that the kabalas were stolen but as there was no such case in the pleading the said deposition can not be taken into consideration, that averments made as to cause of action are not true, that in the totality of the facts it appear that Ext.4 by which plaintiffs said to have purchased the land in suit is not genuine, that from Exts. (a) and (b) it is seen that the land in suit is fishery and the Government auctioned the same and thus it is seen that the land in suit is not boro land, that plaintiffs have not acquired any right, title and interest in the land in suit on the basis of their allege purchases since the land is fishery vested with the Government on the acquisition of rent receiving interest. On the aforesaid findings the trial Court dismissed the suit. The appellate Court upon reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court allowed the appeal and decreed the suit on the findings that from the Government's side no paper was produced to show that the land in suit was fishery and on the acquisition of rent receiving interest the same vested in the Government and as regard the land in suit no C.A. Roll was prepared and as such interest in the land in suit remains with the tenant and consequent thereupon the plaintiffs by their purchase from the recorded tenants acquired right, title and interest in the land in suit, that S.A. record Ext.5 was prepared without any basis.
case_type_name: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal

lawyer:
Md Khalilur Rahman, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners. 
SRM Lutfor Rahman Akand, Advocate ----- For the Respondent No.4
parties:
Zahirul Islam & others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Ashfaqul Islam J: At the instance of the petitioners, this Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondent to show cause as to why the impinged 8 (eight) notices dated 1-2-2003 issued under the signature of respondent No.3 for rehearing of Settlement Appeal Case Nos. 2846, 2847, 2849, 2850, 2857, 2858, 2859 and 3025 of 1999 with a reference to Miscellaneous Case No. 760 of 2002 (Annexure-E, E (1), E(2), E(3), E(4), E(5), E(6) and E(7) should not be declared to have been passed illegally and without lawful authority and why direction should not be issued to send the draft publication of Khatian Nos. 237, 155, 125 and 245 of Mouza Shantinagar, Police Station Motijheel, Dhaka prepared in the name of the petitioners to the Settlement Press for final publication. 

 2. Facts leading to the issuance of the present Rule, in short, are that after completing all the stages of proceeding for survey and settlement of recent Mohanagari settlement under relevant Rules of Stale Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 (herein after referred to as SA and T Rules, 1955) (i.e. proceeding known as khanapuri, Bujaral, Attestation, objection and Appeal) 1.20 acres of land covered by DP Khatian No. 237 of Mouza Shantinagar, under Police Station Motijheel, District-Dhaka were recorded in the names of Hazi Zahirul Islam, Jainal Abedin, Hazi Mahbubul Islam, Mojibul Islam (the petitioner Nos. 1, 2, 3, 5) and 8 others, 0.4050 acre of land covered by DP khatian No. 155 were recorded in the name of Hazi Zahirul Islam (The Petitioner No. 1),0.0730 acre land covered by DP Khatian No. 125 were recorded in the name of Kamal Uddin (the petitioner No.4) and 0.0078 acre land covered by DP Khatian No. 245 were recorded in the name of Mojibul Islam (the petitioner No.5). 

 3. The petitioners and their other co-sharers have been owning and possessing a total 1.837 acres of land covered by the aforesaid 4 khatians No. 237, 155, 125 and 245 and some other lands total being 3.21 acres from the time of their predecessors namely Hazi Hafizuddin, Afsaruddin and Md Taher who purchased the 3.21 acres of land including the lands covered by the aforesaid four DP khatian from its lawful owners Bamacharan Pal, Boloram Pal, Hororam Pal and Gupal Chandra Pal by registered sale deed No. 4911 dated 26-8-1952 and have been owning and possessing the same by constructing residential-cum-commercial building. 

 4. While the predecessors of the petitioners were owning and possessing the aforesaid 3.21 acres of land along with the building thereon, including the land covered by aforesaid four I) DP Khatians, the then Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT) issued notice for requisition of 2.19 acre of land including the land covered by 4 khatians for the purpose of acquisition for constructing North-South Road by starting LA Case Nos. 8/65-66 through the ADC (LA) Dhaka. Subsequently the aforesaid 2.19 acre of land was de-requisitioned by notice dated 24th April 1968. 

 5. The land covered by the order of derequisition as well as of 4 DP Khatians as mentioned above were wrongly recorded in the name of Collector, Dhaka as khas land but at the time of preparation of RS record the land in question' was duly and correctly ordered to be recorded in the name of petitioner No.5 and the predecessors of other petitioners and other co-sharers in Settlement Appeal Case No.1 53 and accordingly RS and DP khatian No. 53 was prepared though the respondent No.4 did not participate in any proceeding under Rules 28 to 31 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act Rules 1955 at the time of operation of RS record of right before the survey and settlement authority but fraudulently entered his name in the said RS Khatian at the time of final publication in collusion with the staffs of the Settlement Press and on the basis of the said fraudulent RS khatian managed to have recorded his name in the recent Mohanagari Record of Right against which the petitioners and others filed Objection Case Nos. 10, 12,61,40,41,43,57,24, 0,46,44,47,48,42,28,25,22 and 69 under Rule 30 of SA and T Rules, 1955. The objection officer heard both the parties and allowed the objection Case Nos. 10 and 12 by analogous judgment dated 23-6-1999. 

 7. It is further stated that after the judgment given in the appeal cases under, Rule 31 there is no provision other than to send the DP khatian to the settlement Press for final publication .under Rule 32 of SA and T Rules, 1995 and the petitioners were waiting for such finally published khatian but all on a sudden on 3rd February 2003 the petitioners obtained separated 8 notices issued under the signature of Settlement Officer, Dhaka, the respondent No.3 dated 1-2-2003 for re-hearing of the self name appeal Case Nos. 2846/99, 2847/99, 2849/99, 2850/99, 2857/99, 2858/99, 2859/99 and 3025/99 under Rule 31 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 by giving a reference of Miscellaneous case No. 760 of 2002. It is at this state the petitioner moved this Division under Article 102 of the constitution and obtained the present Rule. 

 8. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioners after taking us with the petition, the impugned notices and other annexure with the petition, mainly pressed that the impugned notices dated 1-2-2003 for re-hearing of the appeal Case Nos. 2846/99, 2847/99, 2849/99, 2850/99, 2857/99, 2858/99, 2859/99 and 3025/99 afresh has been issued. Without any lawful authority and without jurisdiction which should be declared unconstitutional. In elaborating his argument the learned Advocate submits that the notices for re-hearing of the appeal cases is absolutely in violation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules; 1955. He submits that once the appeal has been disposed on contest under Rule 31 no review or other, application lies and settlement authority has no jurisdiction to re-open the mailer other than to send the draft application khatian for final publication in the settlement press under Rule 32 of the SA and T Rules, 1955. This is well settled as he submits. In support of his contentions he placed reliance on the decision of Romisa Khanam vs Bangladesh 61 DLR 18, (where one of us was a party), Md Abtab Ali Sheikh vs Director of Land Records 11 MLR 226 and Capital Co-operative Housing Society Ltd vs Bangladesh 45 DLR 289. 

 "In the scheme of revision of a record-of- rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 there are various stages laid down in the Rules, 1955. After completion of attestation the Revenue Officer shall under Rule 29 published the draft record-of-rights for public inspection. Under Rule 30, the Revenue Officer shall decide summarily in presence of the interested parties any objection regarding ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land. Any person aggrieved by such an order on any objection made under Rule 30 may appeal to the Revenue Officer appointed with additional designation of Settlement Officer or of Assistant Settlement Officer commonly known as Appellate Officer within 30 days from the date of order appealed against. Any order passed on such appeal appears to be final as no further appeal or revision is provided there from. 

 After disposal of the objections under Rule 30 and appeals under 31 and correction of the draft record-of-rights in accordance with the original and appellate orders on all objections, the Revenue Officer shall proceed to frame final record of rights under Rule 31 and then, publish record of rights under Rule 33. Under Rule 34, the Revenue Officer shall within sixty days of the final publication make a certificate stating the fact of such final publication and the date thereof, etc. And the Government by a notification in the official gazette may declare with regard to any specified area that the record-of-rights has been finally published for every village included in such area and such notification shall be conclusive proof of such publication. 

 Chapter VIII of said Rules, 1955 deals with general power of Revenue Officer in revising record-of-rights under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 Rule 42 gives special power to a Revenue Officer appointed with additional designation of Settlement Officer to direct at any time before the publication of the final record of rights that any portion of the proceedings referred to in Rule 28 to 32 in respect of any district, part of a district or local area shall be cancelled and the proceedings shall be taken up fresh from such stage as he may direct. Similarly, such Settlement Officer is empowered under Rule 42A upon an application or receipt of an Official Report to correct any entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-right before final publication, and after consulting the relevant records and making such other enquiries as he deems necessary, to direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to an appeal. At the same time, the Revenue Officer shall make the correct entry after hearing the parties and record his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference. But none of such powers under Rule 42 or 42A of the Rules, 1955 appears to empower such Settlement Officer to sit and or act as an appellate authority over an appellate order passed under Rule 31 and set-aside such, appellate order or direct the Appellate Officer to hear an appeal afresh in respect of a particular holding. Nor the Appellate Officer is empowered to rehear an appeal which was finally disposed by him. The Settlement Officer therefore most illegally cancelled the appellate orders and compelled the Appellate Officer to hear the appeals afresh." 

 12. Against this decision Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate who was the respondent in the said case unsuccessfully moved the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 1447-52 of 2008. The Appellate Division finally set at rest of the same once for all. All other decisions as referred to above are on the same point and all these decisions settled the proposition of law that once appeal has been disposed of on contest under Rule 31 of Sate Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 no review or other application lies and the settlement authority have got no jurisdiction to re-open the mater other than to send the draft publication khatian for final publication under Rule 32 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955. Even Rule 42 does not empower the Settlement Officer to sit and act as an appellate authority over an appellate order passed under Rule 31 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules 1955. In that view of the matter, this Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned 8 (eight) notices dated 1-2-2003 issued under the signature of respondent No.3, the Settlement Officer is hereby declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and, as such, no legal effect and it is also directed to send the draft publication khatian Nos. 237, 155, 125 and 245 of Mouza Shantinagar, Police Station Motijheel, Dhaka prepared in the name of the petitioners to the settlement press for final publication.
