full_judgment:
2. The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.68 of 1999.in the court of the Senior Assistant Judge. Dacupe, Khunla imploding the opposite parties as defendants praying for declaration that the order passed in Miscellaneous Case No.1 of 1998-99 by the defendant No.4 declaring the suit land as government khas and is illegal, null and void, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiffs and for a permanent injunction alleging, inter alia, that one Rameswar and others were the owners in possession of 20.26 acres of land which was sold in Certificate Case No.358/61-62 of the office of the Certificate Officer, Khulna and the plaintiff No. 1 auction purchased the 15 annoy share of the said property and the defendant Nos.7 and 8 purchased 10 gondas share each in open auction held on 30.5.1962 and the sale was 2008 confirmed on 30.7.1962 and auction purchasers got sale Certificate on 22.9.1962 and they got delivery of possession of the suit land through process of law and then mutated their names in the S.A. khatian Vide Mutation Case No.9 of 1965 and they arc in possession on payment of rent to the Government. It is further alleged that the plaintiffs auction purchaser transferred some lands to other plaintiffs who are in possession of 19.99 acres of land out of the holding. It is also alleged that one Kesto Majhee instituted Title Suit No.380 of 1963 in the Second Court of the then Munsif, Khulna for setting aside the auction sale but the said suit was ultimately dismissed on compromise. Thereafter one Durlov Chandra Roy and 5 others as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.259 of 1966 in the Second Court of the then Munsif, Khulna against one Rakhal Chandra Mondal and 11 others including. the present petitioner No. 1 Mollick Ali Ahmed and the opposite party Nos. 7 and 8 Rashid Uddin Ahmed and Arun Kanti Banajee in respect of 1.65 acres of land out of the suit holding and obtained exparte decree on 14.2.1967 and that subsequently Use present petitioner No. 1 and opposite party Nos.7 and 8 instituted Title Suit No.3I4 of 1969 in the Second Court of the then Munsif, Khulna for declaration that the exparte decree passed in Title Suit No.259 of 1966 was fraudulent, illegal and void and obtained a contested decree. One Durlov Chandra Roy and others filed Title Appeal No.124 of 1973 against the said decree which upon contesting hearing was dismissed and the decree setting aside the exparte judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.259 of 1966 was affirmed. Thereafter one Nilkanta Mondal as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.770 of 1980 against the plaintiffs and others for declaration of title in respect of 5.96 acres of land out of the entire auction purchased land of S.A. khatian No.330 in the First Court of the then Munsif, khulna which was ultimately dismissed on 7.1.1990. There after one Naren Majhee filed an application before defendant No.3 (Than Nirbahi Officer) against Ramjan Mollick and other bargadars of the plaintiffs which was numbered as Miscellaneous Case No.43 of 1990 and as Naren Majhee was found absent on the date fixed for hearing the said case was dismissed and thereafter Naren Majhee instituted Title Suit No.94 of 1996 for partition in respect of 4.6250 acres of land out of the suit holding in the 2nd Court of the Assistant Judge, Dacupe which was subsequently transferred to the court of the Assistant Judge. Fultala and was re-numbered as Title Suit No.25 of 1998 and ultimately the said suit was dismissed for non-prosecution on 7.6,1998. It is further alleged that suddenly the defendant No.2, A.D.C. Khulna passed an order in Miscellaneous Case No.3 of 1996 making the entire auction purchased land as government khas land against which the plaintiffs and defendant No.7 and 8 filed Appeal No.334 of 1996 before the Additional Divisional Commissioner (Revenue) Khulna Division who allowed the appeal and directed Additional Deputy Commissioner, Khulna (defendant No.2) to dispose of the matter according to law and meanwhile directed to maintain status quo in respect of the auction purchased land. The defendant No.2 by his order dated 25.2.1996 again allowed the entire auction purchased land as government khas land and the plaintiff again preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.5 who allowed the appeal, set aside the order dated 25.2.1996 and directed to dispose of the matter in the light of the observation made in the order dated 24.3.1996 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No.334 of 1996. A further appeal was taken being Appeal No.27 of 1997-98 to the defendant No.6, Member-2, Land Appeal Board, Segun Bagicha, Dhaka who by his order dated 28.8.1997 sent the case back on remand to the defendant No.2 and thereafter the defendant No.2 sent the case to defendant No.4 Assistant Commissioner of Land, Dacupe with a direction to dispose of the case upon starting a Miscellaneous Case. The defendant No.4 accordingly started Miscellaneous Case No.1 of 1998-99 under Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and passed an order on 1.4.1999 making 15.6350 acres of land of S.A. Khatian No-330 as government khas land leaving aside 4.6250 acres of land in favour of Naren Majhee. It is stated that the initiation of the proceeding of Miscellaneous Case No. 1/88-89 and all other subsequent actions are wholly illegal, void and of no legal effect and that no notice of the said proceeding was served upon the plaintiffs and the said proceeding and the order are not binding on the plaintiffs. It is also alleged that the plaintiffs never abandoned their residence on the suit land and that they are in 'possession of the entire auction purchased land along with defendant Nos.7 and 8 and that the suit and can not vest in the government as khas land and instituted the suit. 

 4. The defendant No. 1 in its written statement alleged that the suit property was found without any owner and 37.00 acres of land appertaining to C.S Khatian No.98 of mouza Sutar Khali under Police. Station Dacope belonged to Tarak Chandra Majhi. Gaur Chandra Majhi and Rakhal Majhi to the extent of 4 annas share each and to Shanyashi Mondol, Shibnath Mondal, Puma Charan Mondal, Haran Chandra Mondal and Ratikanta to the extent of 16 gondas shares each and the same was recorded in the R.S Khatian No.285 in the names of the descendants of those recorded owners including some of the aforesaid persons and that the said property was recorded in the finally published S.A. khatian No.330 in the name of Rameswar, Gaur Chandra, Rakhal, Shannyashi, Puma Charan, Ratikanta and others and that one Jiban Krishna Majhee and others, one set of the recorded tenants got 16.74 acres of .land separated and recorded in S.A. khatian Nos.330(I), 330(2) and 330(3) and the remaining 20.26 acres of land remained in the original S.A. Khatian No.330 in the . names of Rameswar and others and that-the recorded tenant Gaur Chandra Majhee while owning and possessing 4.6250 acres of land, died leaving behind his only son Kesto Majhee who has been possessing his property inherited from his father and that 15.63 acres of land is owner less which was made government khas land in terms of report of the Tahsildar tinder Section 92(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on .6.9.1994 against which appeal was filed and ultimately the matter was sent to the Additional Deputy Commissioner for final disposal and accordingly the. Additional Deputy Commissioner sent the matter to the Assistant Commissioner (Land). Dacope who started Miscellaneous Case No.1 of 1998-99 under Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and served notice upon both the parties and by order dated 1.4.1999 made 15.63 acres of land as government khas land and granted lease of the said property to the lessees in the year 1405 B.S. in Miscellaneous Case No.37/98-99, 38/98-99, 31/98-99, 32/98-99 and 40/98-99 and that the lessees are in possession of the suit land within the knowledge of the plaintiffs. It is further alleged that one Ruhul Amin Gazi and others had also taken the lease of the suit land and the plaintiffs did not implead them in the suit. It is further alleged that one Nilkanta Mondal as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.770 of 1980 against the plaintiff No. 1 and others for declaration of title which was dismissed with costs though they filed a solenama with defendant No. 1 claiming the suit property as auction purchased property but the same was rejected and the property was declared to be vested and non-resident property by the order of the court dated 30.11.1989. It is also asserted that the defendant No.9-19 are in actual possession of the suit land and that the story of auction sale is false, baseless and the plaintiffs have instituted the suit in order to grab the suit property. 

 5. The defendant Nos.9- 19 field another written statement reiterating the state-meats made by the defendant No. I in its written statement and further contending that they being the landless cultivators got lease of the suit land for the year 1403 B.S. and then again for the year 1405 B.S. and they are in possession of the suit land which is government khas land and prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 9. Mr. M Quamrul Hoque Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has taken me through the judgments of the courts below and submits that the courts below made a wrong approach to the pleadings of the parties and the evidence on record and failed to notice that the plaintiffs acquired a valid title on the basis of auction purchase of the suit land in May 1962 and that they are in possession of the suit land upon mutating their names and on payment of rents to the government. Mr. Siddique further submits that both the courts below committed a gross error of law in holding that sale certificate in respect of an auction is- not a deed of title. Mr. Siddique has referred to Section 20 of the Public Demands Recovery Act and submits that whatever title the certificate debtor had in the property at the time of auction sale shall pass to the auction purchaser and the sale certificate is a document of title. Mr. Siddique has further submitted that the defendant No. 1 claimed the suit land on the basis of escheat under Section 92 of State Acquisition and Tenancy At and that the onus is on the government to prove that the last owner died intestate. Id support of his submission Mr. Siddique relied on a decision in the case of Geeta Rani alias Shamima Khatun Vs. Bangladesh reported in 36 DLR(AD)225. The learned Advocate further submits that the government could not produce any evidence that the recorded owners died intestate leaving behind no heir to attract the provision of Sub-section 1(a) of Section 92 of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act. It is also submitted that the government did not disclose the flame of the raiyot whose interest has been extinguished and the property stood escheat to the government. Mr. Siddique further invited my attention to Sub-section 2 and 3 of Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act read with the evidence of D.W.3, a Thasilder of the concerned Thasil Office to show that no notice, as required under Sub-section 3 of Section 92, was published in the prescribed manner declaring the intention of the Revenue Officer to enter on the holding with specific reason thereof. According to Mr. Siddique there is complete non-compliance of the requirement of Sub-section 2 of Section 92 of the. State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which provides that when the interest of Raiyot in a holding is extinguished under Sub- section (1), the Revenue Officer may enter on-the holding; and the holding shall, with effect from the date on which the Revenue Officer so enters on it, Vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances. According to the learned Advocate there is no vesting of the suit land in the government and as such the impugned alleged older dated 1.4.1999 was never acted upon. The learned Advocate has further submitted that the mutated khatian and the rent receipts Ext.1.2-12 (Tha) including the chowkidary taxes exhibit 13-13(f) and the Government ledger for collection of rents which was marked Ext. 28 by the appellate court as  additional evidence clearly indicates that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land and that they are entitled to a decree for permanent injunction. The learned Advocate submits that the courts below while deciding the question of possession and title totally ignored the aforesaid evidence and also misread the, evidence of D.W.3 who admitted that no notice was issued or served on the certificate purchasers before the suit land was made government khas land. The learned Advocate has also relied on a decision in the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Manikgonj Vs. Md. Siddiqur Rahman and others reported in 46 DLR(AD) 179 in support of his submission that the mutated khatian and rent receipts are evidence of possession. According to the learned Advocate, the order declaring the property as government khas land being without lawful authority in the absence of the compliance of the legal requirement of service of notice and affording hearing of the auction purchasers, the limitation as provided in Section 92(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shall not govern the case but it shall govern under Article 120 of the Limitation Act. In any view, the learned Advocate submits that both the courts below committed a serious error of law in the impugned decision which has resulted in a miscarriage of justice. 

 11: Mr. H.N. Nondy, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the lessees, who are defendant Nos.9- 19, adopts the submissions of the learned Assistant Attorney General and adds that the lessees being in possession of the suit land, the suit without any prayer for a consequential relief is not maintainable under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Mr. Nondy submits that the contesting defendant Nos.9-19 has produced large number of DCR showing payment of premium to the government for the suit land which show that they are in possession of the suit land which has been supported by the evidence of D.W.1-3 and on the face of this material evidence the suit for permanent injunction was not maintainable. Mr. Nondy further submits that the suit is barred by limitation as it was not filed within 90 days from the date of the order making the suit land as the khas land under Sub-section 4 of Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and ultimately submits that concurrent finding of fact on title and possession may not be disturbed by this revisional court. 

 12. 1 have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for all the parties and perused the impugned judgments and all other evidence on record. Ext. 1 is the C.S. khatian which shows that Tarak Chandra Majhee, Gaur Chandra Majhee and Rakhal Chandra Majhee were recorded as owners to the extent of 4 annas shares each and Shanyashi Mondal, ShibNath Mondal, Purna Charan Mondal, Haran Chandra Mondal and Ratikanta Mondal were also recorded in respect of 16 gondas share each. This EXt. 1 relates to C.S. Khatian No.98 which correspondents to S.A. Khatian No.330. Ext.4 is the original copy of the sale certificate in Certificate Case No.358/61-62 filed by province of East Pakistan being certificate holder against ( I ) Rameswar son of Tarak Chandra Mazi (II) Sannashi (III) Puma Chandra (IV) Rati Kanta son of Kalicharan Mandal of Sutarkhali at present in India. (V)Gourchandra son of Shyama Charan Mazi (VI) Rakhal Son of Baisnab Mazi of Sutarkhali, P.S: Dacope, Khulna as certificate debtors and it shows that an area of 20.26 acres was sold in public auction on 30.5.1962 for Rs. 515/- only in execution of Certificate Case No.358/61-62. This sale certificate was granted under the signature of the certificate officer, Chalna, Khulna dated 27.9.62. Ext.4  is again the paper showing delivery of possession to certificate purchasers and khatian number is not readable but the total area shows therein measures 20.26 acres and delivery of possession was given on 5.10.62 by one Dhirendra Nath being the process server of the. R.C.O. Office, Chalna. Ext.3 is the mutated S.A. khatian which shows that in view of the order passed in Mutation Case No.9/65 the S.A. Khatian No.330 was corrected and mutated in the names of auction purchasers on the basis of the order dated 19.6.1965. Section 20 of the Public Demands Recovery Act provides that where property is sold in execution of a certificate, the title shall vest in the purchaser which is merely the right, title and interest of the certificate debtor at the time of the sale, even though the property itself be specified. Sub-section 2 of Section 20 provides that where immovable property is sold in execution of a certificate, and such sale has become absolute, the purchaser's right, title and interest shall be deemed to have vested in him from the time when property is sold, and not from the time when the sale becomes absolute. This section 20 Sub-section land 2 of the Public Demands Recovery Act indicates that the auction purchasers interest become absolute from the date of auction sale held on 30.5.62 and from that date whatever title the certificate debtors had in the auction sold property shall pass to the auction purchasers. It may be remembered that this auction sale took place at the instance of the province of East Pakistan being the certificate holder. Government now by only saying that the auction sale was fraudulent can not be absolved, from discharging their onus to prove with cogent and sufficient evidence that the auction sale was not Feld at the instance of the government or that there was illegality and irregularity in the conduct of auction sale and that it was not a proper transaction. Upon a consideration of the entire evidence and the pleadings of the parties I do not find any attempt made by the government to prove that the auction sale of the property was a fraudulent one; not taken at the instance of the government as the certificate holder. I do not find any other material excepting an assertion that the auction sale is fraudulent but such assertion on the face of the original sale certificate Ext. 4 and writ of delivery of possession is not sufficient to demolish the auction sale of the property which took place on 30.5.1962 and same government on the basis of the said auction sale mutated the khatian in the name of the auction purchasers Ext.3. The suit land appertaining to S.A. Khatian No.330 could not be treated as escheat property and on the face of Ext. 3 the recorded tenants, who are the auction purchasers, are paying rents for the auction purchased properties by Ext.l2-12 (Tha) and the Chowkidary tax receipt vide Ext. 13-13(M). The government ledger of collection of rents which was produced before the appellate court and marked Ext.28 by the appellate court shows that rents for the auction purchased properties have been paid up to date and there is no arrear. The appellate court though accepted this ledger as Ext.28 as called for by its order No.11 dated 22-3-2001 did not consider this material document Ext.28 while holding that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their exclusive possession in the suit land overlooking that payment of rents is good piece of evidence in support of possession. This is the view taken by our Appellate Division in the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216. Apart from Ext. 12 series and 13 series, Ext.3 is again a vital document to prove-plaintiffs possession in the suit land. Ext.3 is the mutated khatian in the name of the plaintiffs. It is true that Ext.27 is a true copy of the S.A. Khatian and it was not admissible in evidence as it was not certified copy and was not obtained in due process of law but a certified copy of the said mutated khatian was legally proved and marked Ext.3. Since the government claims that the suit land became escheat let me now consider how far the government has proved that the last owner had died intestate leaving behind no heir to attract Sub-section 1(a) of Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the plea was raised by the Government-defendant and onus lies on it to prove the same. Ext. I being the C.S. khatian shows several names as C.S. recorded tenants. Ext.6 is the order passed in Title Suit No.380 of 1963 instituted by Kesto Majhee against the auction purchaser Raisuddin Ahmed. Order dated 25.11.65 shows that the suit was dismissed in terms of the solenama against defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and for non-prosecution against the rest. The solenama is Ext.7 which shows that Kesto, Majhee accepted the auction sale of the suit property and assured that he would not make any claim in respect of the suit land. This Kesto Majhee is a son of .C.S. recorded owner Gam. Chandra Majhee. Naren. Chandra Majhee, a son of Kesto Majhee instituted Title Suit No.94 of 1996 against the auction purchasers and others and the said suit was ultimately dismissed for non prosecution. There was another suit filed by one Durlov Majhee being Title Suit No.259 of 1966 which was decreed exparte vide judgment and decree Ext. 1 Subsequently the auction purchasers instituted Title Suit No.314 of 1969 in the 3rd Court of the then Munsif, Khulna for setting asi4 the said exparte decree passed in Title Suit No.259 of 1966 which was decreed on contest by judgment Ext.l0. There are other suits which all were ultimately dismissed but none of them excepting Title Suit No.314 of 1969 was instituted by the auction purchasers as plaintiffs. In none of the said suits the government was made a party as the government was not a necessary party in those suits. The government filed written statement in the present suit on 14.3.2000 when they learnt about the auction sale but did not take any steps to set aside the auction sale as yet. In Miscellaneous Case No. t of 1998-99 the suit land was ordered to be made government khas land as it was found without any owner, presumably under Section 92 (1)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which provides that the interest of a raiyat in a holding shall be extinguished when he dies intestate leaving no heir entitled to inherit under the law of inheritance to which he is subject. The order passed in Miscellaneous Case No: 1/98-99 does not show the interest of which raiyot in the holding was extinguished and which raiyot had died intestate leaving no heir. Our appellate Division in 36 DLR(AD) 225 took the view while construing section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act The onus is on the Government to prove that the last owner died intestate. In this case the defendant Government of Bangladesh claim the property by way of escheat since Gour Dasi died intestate without leaving any heir according to it. When the claim is founded on escheat the onus lies on the Government to show that the owner of the estate died without heir." On an examination of the written statement I could not find out the disclosure of the name of any raiyot of the holding who had died intestate leaving behind no heir to inherit the property and the property became escheat to the government. In the absence of any assertion or any evidence in that behalf the government is not permitted to treat a property as escheat and became government khas land under Section 92(1)(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Further, before taking any such steps the Revenue Officer shall cause a notice to be published, in the prescribed manner declaring his intention to enter on the holding and specifying the reason thereof and also inviting objections from all persons interested in the holding and shall consider any objection that may be submitted to him within the period specified in that behalf in the-notice and shall record a decision There is complete absence of pleading of this mandatory provision of Sub-section 3 of section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. There is no evidence before the court that the Revenue Officer caused any notice published in the prescribed manner before he took the decision. The Revenue Office is again required to enter on the land in order to complete the vesting of the property in the government as khas land and to this item also there is no evidence that the Revenue Officer at any time entered on the suit land and complied with the provisions of Sub-section 2 of Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. D.W.3 Hasanuzzaman Sarder deposed as Office Assistant of Dacope land Office. In his cross-examination he stated " …..১১/৮/৯৮ তারিখ এর আদেশে উভয় পক্ষকে নোটিশ দিন লেখা আছে। ২৫/৮/৯৮ তারিখ এ এস,আর ফেরৎ আসে নাই লেখা আছে। ঐ আদেশে বিবাদীর প্রতি নোটিশ জারি হয়ে ফেরত আসে নাই লেখা আছে। নোটিশ জারী হয়ে ফেরত এসেছে একথা কোথাও লেখা নেই। পক্ষদ্বয় বাদী বিবাদী। এরে বলে বিবাদমান দুটি পক্ষ। কে প্রার্থনা করেছে এই কথা রেকর্ডেও কোথায়ও লেকা নাই। ---১৮/১০/৯৮ তাং এর আদেশে আলী আহম্মদের পক্ষে নিয়োজিত এ্যাডঃ হাজিরা দিয়েছেন লেখা আছে। এ্যাডঃ সাহেবের নাম নাই। ওকালতনামা নাই। The evidence of D.W.3 clearly indicates that no notice was served before the suit land was declared as government land though it is the mandatory provisions of law that notice has to be served before taking such a decision. Apart from all this factual aspects, another vital facts have been missed by both the courts below. In the mutated khatian Ext.3 the names of the auction purchasers have been recorded with effect from 19.3.1965. By this mutated khatian the names of the auction purchasers Rashid Uddin Ahmed Mallick Uddin Ahmed and Arun Kanti Benarjee were recorded and it is not the case of the government that any one of the said S.A. recorded tenants died intestate leaving behind no heir to inherit the property and their right was therefore extinguished. This mutation was- also ordered by the government. This exhibit 3 shows that the certificate sale was acted upon and the government accepted the certificate sale and mutated the names of the certificate purchasers in the connected khatian and allowed mutation. Government is not now permitted to deny the acceptance of the auction purchasers as the tenants in respect of the suit land appertaining to S.A. khatian No.330. Both the courts below ignored to consider this material facts and this aspect of the case was totally ignored while mainlining the order passed in -Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1998-99. Both the court have concurrently recorded a finding of fact that the plaintiffs suit land as government khas land was unauthorised and illegal, the suit shall be govern under Article 120 of the Limitation Act and not under Sub-section Section 4 of Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This will also bring as to decide the question of possession. The government did not take over possession at any time as there is no evidence that the Revenue Officer ever entered upon the suit land after declaring the same as government khas land in terms of Sub-section 2 of Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The government however allegedly granted eksona lease to defendant Nos.9-l9 and also to few others. Thus eksona lease for one year was therefore illegal and without jurisdiction and the government is under legal obligation to restore possession from its lessees to the S.A. recorded owners meaning thereby the lessees acquired no interest in the suit land and they were mere temporarily yearly lessees and they are liable to vacate the suit land as and when the government including the ' local concerned authority who are opposite party Nos.2-4, no directs them. These eksona lessees are in unauthorised possession and under a legal obligation to restore possession to the government and in the presence of the government they are not necessary parties in the suit, as held by the trial court. In the facts of the case the suit is not barred under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The petitioners are therefore entitled to get a decree in part. 

 13. In the result this rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 18.4.2002 passed by the First Court of the Additional District Judge, Khulna in Title Appeal No.394 of 2000 affirming those date 27.9.2000 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Dacope, Khulna in Title Suit No.68 of 1999 dismissing the suit are hereby set aside. The suit is decreed in part. It is declared that the order passed in Miscellaneous Case No.1 of 1998-99 by the defendant No.4 declaring the suit land as government khas land is malafide, illegal, null and void and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs prayer for perpetual injunction is dismissed.

2. The facts relevant for the disposal of this Rule in brief are that, the opposite parties being plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No. 125 of 1991 in the court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Naogaon for declaration of title in the suit land, contending inter alia that the suit land originally belonged to Niroda Sundari and Dasya in equal share  Mrinalini Dasya orally relinquished her share in favour of Niroda Sundari who became the owner of 16 annas share in the suit land. On 23.6.1947 Niroda Sundari sold the same to one Haider Ali by a registered sale deed No. 3142. Thereafter Haider Ali sold the suit land to the plaintiff No. 1-2 through registered sale deed dated 29.8.1968 and handed over possession to them. to ignorance of Haider Ali thy land was wrongly recorded in the name of Niroda Sundari in S. A. Khatian. Since the Patnitola Sub-registrar's Office was burnt during war of liberation they could not obtain original copy of the sale deed and as such they have filed the certified copy of the aforesaid deed, which was obtained before war of liberation. During R. S. operation it was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendants along with the names of the plaintiffs and quantum of land in R.S. Plot No. 221 was recorded as 1.17 acres in place of 1.77 acres of land. The R.S. record was wrong. 

 3. The defendant petitioners herein contested the suit by filing written statement denying material allegations made in the plaint, contending inter alia, that admittedly Niroda Sundari was the original owner of the suit land and the plain-tiffs' father and the father of the defendants were full brothers who purchased the suit land in the name of the plaintiffs and the defendants as well, in equal share and in R.S. Khatian the land was correctly recorded in their names. 

 6. He further submits that the courts below arrived at an erroneous decision that the plaintiffs have mutated their names, though no papers was filed in support of their contention. As per him the S.A. Khatian was finally published in the year 1965 and the deed of transfer in favour of Haider Ali alleged to have been registered on 23.6.1947 but Haider Ali did not take any steps to rectify the S.A. Khatian which was prepared and published in the name of Niroda Sundari. 

 10. It appears from the plaint that the plaintiffs claimed their title by purchase of the suit land from one Haider Ali, who purchased the same from Niroda Sundari and they have claimed that the R.S. record was wrong and in R.S. Plot No. 221 of Khatian No. 35, the quantum of land was recorded as 1.17 acres in place of 1.77 acres of land. It appears from the written statement filed by the Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 that they claimed their title through purchase from Niroda Sundari by their father and uncle, the father of the plain-tiffs, jointly. In paragraph No. 6 of their written statement they have stated that their father died in the year 1964-65. In paragraph No. 9 of the written statement they have claimed that the deed of title of the plaintiffs was forged, which the Defendant No. 1 would prove at the time of trial and also prayed for impounding the certified copy of the sale deed, being filed by the plaintiff. In paragraph 14 of the written statement the defendants claimed that while their father and the father of the plaintiffs were in joint Mess they have purchased the suit land in the names of their respective sons from Niroda. Sundari in equal share.

Thereafter Abdus Sobhan died leaving son Abdus Samad, daughter Aroba Khatun and wife Nasua Khatun to succeed him. The aforesaid owners being in rightful possession of the case Land sold 22 decimals of Land to pre-emptee petitioner Abdul Latif Bhuiyan land the predecessor-in-interest or opposite parties Nos. 7-11, Abdul Latif Bhuiyan subsequently purchased the aforesaid 0.22 decimals of land by kabalas dated 27-7-1964 in the name of his wife Tarina Akhter Khatun. The case of the plaintiffs briefly are that the .486 decimals of land of the disputed joth was originally belonged to Jafar Ali, who died intestate leaving behind 2(two) sons, Roshan Ali and Abdul Hamid Ali and a daughter Saberunnessa as his legal heirs. During the State Acquisition Settlement, in the year 1960, the name of Roshan Ali, Abdul Hamid and their sister were duly recorded and finally published in S.A. Khatian No. 412. The land measuring an area of .105 decimals of plot No. 1303 is part and parcel of the aforesaid land of S.A. Khatian No. 412. The said property of .105 decimals is viti-land and through amicable partition Roshan Ali, predecessor of the plaintiffs got .18 decimals of land adjacent to the south of the graveyard, comprising of .15 decimals of land at the northern side of plot No. 1303. Abdul Hamid got .18 decimals of land to the adjacent south of Roshan Ali and thereafter, Roshan Ali again got .6 decimals at the adjacent south of Abdul Hamid. Accordingly, Roshan Ali’s .18 decimals, Abdul Hamid’s .18 decimals and Roshan Ali’s further 6 decimals in total measuring an area of .42 decimals situated at the northern part and adjacent south of the graveyard. While Abdul Hamid was in enjoyment of the aforesaid .18 decimals of land transferred the same to plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 through registered kabala dated 03.01.1977. The plaintiffs being heirs of late Roshan Ali got his aforesaid share (.18+.6) in total .24 decimals of land and by purchase got .18 decimals, and in this way they have acquired title and possession over the aforesaid .42 decimals of land. The defendants have residence adjacent western side of the disputed plot. The sons of Abdul Hamid also sold out their other shares, inherited from their father, to the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs have good title and exclusive possession in the aforesaid property and on being threatened by the defendants to dispossess from the suit land, the plaintiffs instituted the present suit for permanent injunction. Subsequently by way of amendment the plaintiffs amended the plaint, incorporating the fact that after institution of the suit they have been dispossessed by the defendants from .3 decimals of land out of the aforesaid .42 decimals on 15.07.1994. Accordingly, they incorporated an additional prayer for recovery of khash possession, allegedly under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. 

 The Court of appeal below categorically found that the S.A. Khatian No. 412 was prepared in the name of Roshan Ali, Abdul Hamid and Saberunnessa, the sons and daughter of Jafar Ali and also found that the D.W. 1 admitted that there is no evidence that Ala Bakshaw or his son Monsur Ali ever challenged the aforesaid recording in the S.A. Khatian. The Appellate Court also found that the predecessor of the plaintiffs namely, Roshan Ali being son of original C.S. recorded tenant, Jafor Ali have got .18 decimals of land at the northern part of plot No. 1303 adjacent south to the graveyard of .15 decimals of land and Abdul Hamid, another son of Jafor Ali also got .18 decimals of land adjacent south of Roshan Ali’s aforesaid .18 decimals. The said Abdul Hamid through registered kabala dated 03.01.1977 transferred his said .18 decimals of land to the plaintiffs, the deed has been exhibited as Exhibit-‘2’ and Roshan Ali again got .6 decimals at the adjacent south of the aforesaid land. The appellate Court also found that the P.W. 2, 3 and 4 in their evidences categorically supported the claim of P.W. 1 as to the plaintiffs’ possession into the suit land and prior to them, their father and uncle (Abdul Hamid) were in exclusive possession over the said land. The appellate Court below while considering the balance of convenience and inconvenience for granting injunction, categorically found that admittedly no khatian was prepared in the name of Ala Bakshaw, the predecessor-in-interest of defendants and it is also found that the defendants did not claim the property by way of inheritance, but by way of purchase, thus, whether the defendants were inducted into the possession of the property by their vendors before filing of the suit or not or the defendants vendors were in possession or not, is to be proved by the defendants by adducing evidences. The appellate Court also categorically found that the defendant No. 2, Siddiqure Rahman, who examined as D.W. 1, in his cross, admitted that they purchased the property from the southern part of the plot in question from Abdul Hanan, Abdul Malek and Siraj and thus, the defendants by purchasing property from the southern side cannot claim the property at northern side. It is to be noted here that the plaintiffs sought for a permanent injunction regarding an area of .42 decimals of land situated at the northern side of plot No. 1303 out of .105 decimals of land. It is the finding of the appellate Court below that there is no evidence that the Munsur Ali and his 2(two) sons had any possession over the suit land. Referring to the evidence of D.W. 3, appellate Court below also found that the D.W. 3 admitted the .36 decimals of land having been purchased by the defendants are situated at the very southern part. It was also categorically found that the suit was filed on 13.07.1994 by the plaintiffs and the defendants purchased the alleged .36 decimals of land through registered sub-kabala dated 29.10.1994 (Exhibit-‘Umah’) i.e. after filing of the suit. From the aforesaid facts, it appears that the defendants cannot claim that they were in possession over the aforesaid .36 decimals of land prior to filing of the suit, when admittedly the deed was executed and registered on a later date and when the .36 decimals of land situated at the very southern portion of plot No. 1303.

full_judgment:
3. The plaintiff’s case, in short, is that the suit property was the khas land of the Ex Zaminder. The plaintiff took settlement of the same by dint of amalnama (Exhibit-1) in the year of 1333 B.S. The zaminder instituted the Rent Suit No. 582 of 1951 against the plaintiff for arrears of rent wherein the plaintiff paid up the demand by challan (Exhibit-3). Accordingly, S.A khatian was prepared in the name of the plaintiff and thereafter, the plaintiff used to pay rent to the Government. But unfortunately, at the time of Revisional Settlement Operation, the suit land was recorded in the names of both the plaintiff and the defendants. On the basis of the objection petition filed by the plaintiff, the Revenue Officer corrected the MRR and accordingly, recorded the entire land in the name of the plaintiff. But since the plaintiff lived far away from the suit land, the defendants managed to record their names in the RS khatin along with the name of the plaintiff though the plaintiff is the absolute owner of the suit land. He has exclusive possession therein and the RS record created cloudy over the suit land, therefore, the plaintiff constrained to file the aforesaid suit. The defendant contested the suit by filing joint written statements denying the material allegations set out in the plaint contending inter alia that the suit is not maintainable in its present form. 

 4. The defendants’ case is that their father was a Government service holder and he took pattan of the suit land from Brikutsha Estate to this plaintiff as his benamder from his own fund for his own benefit. The plaintiff who was minor had no independent source of income and he did not take pattan and pay rents. During his life time, Naybullah khan possessed the suit land. He died in 1974 leaving behind the plaintiff and the defendants as his legal heirs. The suit land was correctly recorded in the finally published RS khatian. The plaintiff has got no exclusive title and possession in the suit land. And, therefore, the defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 11. The trial Court after considering the entire materials on record held that the plaintiff has got the suit land by way of settlement and he has been possessing the same by paying rent and SA Operation was duly prepared in the name of the plaintiff, but the contention of the defendants is that their father took settlement of suit land from his own fund in the benami of the plaintiff; therefore, onus lies upon them but they hopelessly failed to discharge the burden of proof that their father took settlement in the name of the plaintiff as his benamder. After considering the evidence on record, the trial Court held that the plaintiff has title and possession in the suit land and accordingly, decreed the suit. It is true that father of the plaintiff and defendants did not challenge the settlement made in favour of the plaintiff during his lifetime. The Appellate Court held that Naybullah Khan was a government service holder and he took settlement of the suit land on 18th Jaistha, 1333 BS in the benami of his eldest son Abdul Khan who was at the time a minor boy of 6/7 years of age without any independent source of income or having any independent fund of his own. It is also stated by the Appellate Court since R.S. Khatian was jointly recorded in the name of the plaintiff and defendants; therefore, Appellate Court held the view the predecessor of the plaintiff Nayeb Ullah took settlement of the suit land showing the plaintiff as his benamdar. 

 20. It appears from the record that the father of the plaintiff; Naybullah Khan took settlement of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff-petitioners in 18 Poush, 1333 B.S and S.A record was prepared in the name of the plaintiff and the plaintiff also paid rent to the Government as well as zamindar. It also appears from the record that the plaintiff’s father; Naybullah Khan left this transitory world on 11.01.1974. During his life time i.e within 46 years, Naybullah Khan did not file any suit for declaration that the plaintiff was his benamder nor he raised any question as to the transaction made by him in favour of the plaintiff. S.A khatian was prepared from 1956 to 1962. At that time Naybullah was alive, but he did not raise objection as to S.A khatian. It also appears that all the original documents were produced from the custody of the plaintiff and these documents were admissible as evidence. It is true that the R.S khatian was prepared in favour the plaintiff-petitioners and the defendants jointly and as such, created cloud over the stainless title of the suit land and therefore, the plaintiff was constrained to file a suit for declaration of title and to make a negative declaration that the defendants are not the owners of the suit land. It also appears that since the plaintiff failed to pay rent to the zaminder, the zaminder started rent suit against the plaintiff for realization of the rent in the year of 1951 being Rent Suit No. 582 of 1951 and the plaintiff paid rent to the zaminder. It also appears that during R.S operation, the plaintiff filed objection against the attestation khatian or field survey (মাঠ জরিপ) operation and upon hearing the objection, which were sustained and accordingly the name of the defendants included in the attested khatian had been struck down; but eventually, in collusion with the concerned officials of survey department, the defendants got their names recorded jointly and therefore, the plaintiff was constrained to file the aforesaid suit. Though, for the sake of argument, it is taken as granted that Naybullah Khan got settlment in favour of the plaintiff but his conduct implies that he took settlement for the benefit and welfare of his son; Md. Abdul Wadud Khan. 

 25. On perusal of the oral and documentary evidences, it appears that as per the Rules of preponderance of evidence, the contention of the plaintiff’s possession is heavy in weight but the learned District Judge on slipshod statement held that the joint possession of the plaintiff and the defendants without sifting the documents in entirety. The original documents are lying with the plaintiff and produced from the custody of the plaintiff and those were admitted as evidence without any objection from the defendants’ side. The burden of showing that the alleged transfer is banami transaction has not been discharged by the defendants’ side. Undisputedly, the father of the defendants in his lifetime did not take any legal action against the transaction nor he filed any suit for declaration that the plaintiff was his benamder. Considering the surrounding circumstances, the relationship between the parties and intention and subsequent conduct of Naybullah Khan, it is as clear as daylight that 94 years ago, Naybyllah Khan took settlement of the suit land for the benefit of his eldest son i.e the plaintiff for the purpose of the welfare of his son which is apparent from the subsequent conduct of the Naybullah Khan that means during his lifetime i.e in the span of 43 years did not take any legal action challenging the legality and propriety of the settlement rent suit, S.A khatian and other acts of possession, therefore, the learned District Judge without considering the ramification of the law of banami transaction from boarder perspective illegally held that since Naybullah Khan took settlement from his on fund, therefore, the transaction was benami transaction.

full_judgment:
Md Ali Reza, J: The petitioners in this writ petition obtained Rule Nisi against the impugned order dated 25-7-2022 স্মারক নং উভূঅ/শ্রী/গাজী/বিবিধ ১১৯/২২ passed by respondent 4 in Miscellaneous Case 119 of 2022 correcting the RS khatian 213 and RS plots 2698, 2699, 2700 and 2701 in violation of circular vide Memo No. 31.00.0000.042.67.031.11(Part-1)-343 published by Gazette notification dated 29-7-2021 (Annexure-G) should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. At the time of issuance of the Rule the impugned order was stayed for a period of 3(three) months which was subsequently extended and is still in force. 

 2. The case of the petitioners is that Abdul Mozid, Abdul Aziz, Abdul Gofur and Abdul Johor are owners of 1.98 acres of land of RS plots 2698, 2699, 2700 and 2701 appertaining to RS khatian 213 of Mouza Telihati of Upazila Shreepur. One Shamsul Haq Master who was the predecessor of petitioners 1-3 purchased 0.86 acres from the RS tenants and had been in possession upon mutation and payment of rent from the year 2008. One Abdullah Al Baki also purchased 0.91 acres and mutated his name. Due to illness he executed a power of attorney on 15-6-2022 in favour of petitioner 4. Meanwhile one Sultan Mia and others filed Title Suit 365 of 2019 for declaration of title and recovery of possession and also for partition on 15-9-2019 in respect of 1.98 acres out of 5.70 acres in which petitioner 1 and predecessor of petitioner 4 being defendants 1 and 2 respectively filed written statement on 24-2-2021. In the suit plaintiffs' application for injunction was rejected on 20-3-2022 for want of prima facie case and they along with others filed Miscellaneous Case 119 of 2022 before Assistant Commissioner (Land) Sreepur for correction of RS record 213 on 12-4-2022 on ground of clerical mistake due to wrong entry of the names of the tenants. Assistant Commissioner (Land) who is respondent 4 passed the impugned order on 25-7-2022 in violation of circular published in Additional Gazette on 29-7-2021 and the RS khatian was changed very unfairly in favour of third party on 20-11-2022. Thereafter the plaintiffs of the suit and one Asaduzzaman filed Review Case 60 of 2022 in which predecessors of petitioners 1 and 4 were parties and they for the first time came to know about the proceeding on 21-12-2022 and they also filed two review petitions on 11-1-2023 and 23-1-2023 for setting aside the impugned order dated 25-7-2022. In Review Case 60 of 2022 they filed application for stay all further proceedings of that review case with reference to Title Suit 365 of 2019 now renumbered as 417 of 2021 but respondent 4 did not pay any heed to it. Petitioners 1-3 in the meantime filed an application for their addition in Review Case 60 of 2022 but that was rejected by respondent 4. Respondent 4 had no jurisdiction to pass such impugned order. Respondent 4 exceeded jurisdiction vested upon it and the impugned order dated 25-7-2022 is ultra vires being passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 4. Added respondents 6-8 filed affidavit-in-opposition and contested the Rule. The case of the added respondents 6-8 is that CS tenant Mohim Sheikh transferred 2.20 acres in favour of his wife Moymon Nesa and SA khatian 777 was correctly prepared in her name but RS khatian 213 was mistakenly prepared in the names of the transferors of the petitioners in respect of RS plots 2698, 2699, 2700 and 2701. The successors to Moymon Nesa later on appointed Nurul Islam as their attorney who got ex-parte decree of declaration of title and partition in Title Suit 221 of 2010 and entered into a contract for sale with respondent 7 on 9-8-2010 and in furtherance of the same kabala was registered in favour of respondents 6-8 on 10-1-2022. These respondents along with Asaduzzaman and 17 others had no knowledge about the writ petition and this writ petition suffers defect of party and since the writ petitioners have already filed review against the impugned order this Rule Nisi is liable to be discharged being not maintainable because of availing the statutory remedy. 

 6. On the other hand Mr Faysal Hasan Arif, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of added respondents 6-7 submits that the instant writ petition was filed with a malafide intention to obtain order from this Court as Mr Asaduzzaman and 17 others as well as these respondents despite being necessary parties were not made parties and this Rule Nisi is not maintainable for defect of party. He further submits that the writ petitioners have filed review application before respondent 4 against the impugned order which is still pending thus they are not entitled to have any remedy in writ jurisdiction. He strongly submits that the writ petition is not maintainable because petitioners did not produce the judgment and order dated 25-7-2022 without which the impugned order whether was passed illegally cannot be adjudged and the clerical mistake in khatian which has been corrected was done upon proper exercise of jurisdictional power with lawful authority and the Rule Nisi having no merit is liable to be discharged. 

 9. It transpires from RS record 213 (Annexure-A) that Moymona who was the predecessor and previous owner of both Sultan Mia and others as well as respondents 6-8 has got share in 1.96 acres in RS plot 2596 and on the other side the previous owners of the petitioners were RS tenants Gofur, Johur, Aziz, Mozid in respect of 1.98 acres of land with different shares in different RS plots 2698, 2699, 2700 and 2701. The miscellaneous case was filed for correction of clerical mistake happened in RS record 213 to replace the name of Moymona in place of Gofur and others with reference to annexure-J dated 29-7-2021 which is a circular published in Additional Gazette. The petitioners of the miscellaneous case want to have Moymona's name appearing in column of plot 2576 exchanged with the names of Gofur and others whose different and definite shares have been recorded in plots 2698, 2699, 2700 and 2701 and accordingly the impugned order was passed. This case falls under section 143 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act read with Rule 23(3) of Tenancy Rules, 1955 along with circular published in additional Gazette on 29-7-2021 (Annexure-J). This circular concerns with the clerical mistake in the khatian and deals with such correction under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act read with Rule 23(3) of Tenancy Rules 1955 after serving section 144 to completion. The object of the circular is that the officers empowered and responsible under the law and rules cannot in some cases give the remedy sought by the people to correct the khatian prepared and finally published in the latest survey as they do not have a clear understanding of the purpose of law and this circular aims at giving a clear idea to the officers to properly follow the instructions of the procedure of the provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and Tenancy Rules regarding correction of clerical errors in the khatian. Rule 23(3) of the Tenancy Rules 1955 has been referred to in Clause 3 and clerical mistake is defined in Clause 4 of the circular which shows that a clerical error is an error which is believed to have been made in good faith by mistake or by carelessness and which does not involve the proprietary interest of another person and which if rectified would not impair the interest of another person or diminish or increase the amount of the land. Clause 7 provides mode of correction and sub-clause J is relevant here what says that if in correcting the clerical error in the khatian the ownership is affected to the effect that the amount of the property is reduced or increased and the ownership of another is changed or someone else is benefited or harmed then the revenue officer will have no jurisdiction to correct the khatian and it will be treated as a civil dispute and the action of the Assistant Commissioner will be excluded. The provisions of this circular are very reasonable and equitable and also lawful in the interest of the people and in support of the original law.

lawyer:
Mr A. M Amin Uddin, Senior Advocate instructed by Mrs. Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on Record ------ For the Appellants.

For Respondent Nos.7-10. ------- Not rep-resented.
