lawyer:
Md Khalilur Rahman with Md Khalilur Rahman (Helal)—For the Petitioner. 
Md Alamin Sarker, DAG with KM Masud Rumy, AAG—For Respondents Nos. 3 & 4.
parties:
STS Educational Group Limited ------ Petitioners
vs. 
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar J: This Rule was issued calling upon respondent Nos. 1-9 to show cause as to why the "Amendment Circular" being নং জে প্র্র সিিএল,এ/447(৩) dated 28-8-2010 published in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 7-10-2010 (Annexure-E), issued under the signature of respondent No. 7 wherein the petitioner's 1.10 acres of land under SA Khatian No. 1687 of SA Plot No. 41 corresponding to RS Khatian No. 159 of RS Plot No. 46 of Mouza Sylhet Municipality, PS Sylhet, District-Sylhet has been shown as acquired land under LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64, shall not be declared to have been published without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 3. The entire 1.10 acres of land appertaining to SA Plot No. 41 of SA Khatian No. 1687 of Mouza Sylhet Municipality under Police Station Sylhet Sadar was owned and possessed by Rajani Ranjon Gupta and, as such, his name was duly recorded in the finally published State Acquisition Khatian No. 1687 as owner in possession and, after his death, his only son, Rakkhayani Ranjan Gupta became the owner in possession as his sole legal heir who sold 0.25 acres of land by registered Sale Deed No. 14656 to Md Abdul Moyed, 0.25 acres of land to Md Abdus Shahid by registered Sale Deed No. 14656 on 5-11-1990, 0.20 acres of land to Md Sirajul Islam by registered Sale Deed No. 14700 dated 6-11-1990 and 0.20 acres of land to Musammat Kulsum by registered Sale Deed No. 14701 dated 6-11-1990 and the remaining 0.20 acres of land to Mr Ashis Chowdhury by registered Sale Deed No. 14869 dated 12-11-1990. Out of the aforesaid total 1.10 acres of land, as purchased by the above five persons, Md Abdus Shahid sold his 0.20 acres of land out of his purchased 0.25 acres of land to Md Noor Mia and Md Abdul Ahad (respondent Nos. 10 and 11 respectively) by registered Sale Deed No. 10221 dated 27-8-1995 while the remaining 0.05 acres of land of Md Abdus Shahid was vested in his legal heirs. While the aforesaid owners had been possessing the entire 1.10 acres of land in the above stated mariner, they started to pay land development taxes after mutating their names with the government revenue Office and carried out some development work on the case land including erection of pucca boundary wall, setting up iron gate with the western boundary wall facing the Sagar Dighi Road, Sylhet. 

 4. While the aforesaid owners Md Abdul Moyed and others were thus owning and possessing the aforesaid entire 1.10 acres of land, their mutations were cancelled behind their back vide Miscellaneous Case No. 99 of 1991 and Mutation Khatian No. 7640 was opened in the name of respondent No. 6 who then started to threaten to dispossess Md Abdul Moyed and others from the suit land and, under the circumstances, they filed Title Suit No. 156 of 1991 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar Court, Sylhet for permanent injunction restraining respondent No. 6 and other government officials from disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs in the 1.10 acres of the suit property and also from evicting the plaintiffs therefrom. The suit, being transferred to the Assistant Judge, Circuit Court, Sylhet, was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 20 of 1991 and was decreed on contest on 28-11-1991and upon preferring appeal by respondent No. 6 the same was dismissed on 17-2-2004 and against the said appellate Court's judgment and decree, respondent No. 6 filed Civil Revision No. 4627 of 2004 before the High Court Division, which was also dismissed on contest on 19-4-2007 and, finally, when respondent No. 6 preferred CPLA No. 2041 of 2008 before the Appellate Division the same was dismissed on 14-5-2009 on the ground of limitation. It is stated that, in the aforesaid manner the claim of respondent No. 6 to the case land was finally rejected by the highest Court of this country and, thus, the rightful possession of the petitioners predecessors in the suit property was permanently protected. 

 7. By two sets of affidavits-in-opposition filed on behalf of respondent Nos. 3 and 4 followed by a supplementary affidavit on their behalf, it is stated that the entire 1.10 acres of land, appertaining to SA Plot No. 41 under SA Khatian No. 1687 of Mouza Sylhet Municipality, has been acquired along with other plots, in total 5.59 acres of land, for the establishment of a whole sale fish market vide LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64 but Plot No. 41 was inadvertently dropped from the Gazette Notification published on 4th March, 1965 in Dacca Gazette Part 1 at page 435 by the then officials of the publication department. It is stated that a Notice under section 5(7) of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 was issued vide Sylhet No. 5-25 /63/200-REQN-(111) 25th February, 1965 and the Schedule of the said Notice is as under: 

 9. It is stated that all the awardees were Muslim and no one was of the Hindu faith. Therefore, the claim of owning the 1.10 acres of the acquired land under khatian No. 1687 appertaining to plot No. 41 of Mouza Sylhet Municipality JL No. 91 by Mr Rajani Ranjan Gupta and his son Rukshimini Ranjan Gupta is not true. It is stated that no such person/persons in the name of Rajani Ranjan Gupta and Rukshuini Ranjan Gupta were present at the time of acquisition of the said land as they had left the defunct East Pakistan during the Hindu-Muslim Riot on transfer of their land property to the awardees of the LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64, but the settlement Amla of the EBSA & T Act, 1950 AD had recorded 1.10 acres of land under Khatian No. 1687 appertaining to plot No. 41 in the name of Rajani Ranjan Gupta in their absence, which enticed the land grabbers of the Sylhet town to make one fake Rukshini Ranjan Gupta son of late Rajani Ranjan Gupta and successfully transferred lands in favour of (1) Mr Abdus Shahed, 0.25 acres, (2) Mr Abdul Moyed, 0.25 acres, (3) Md Sirajul Islam, 0.20 acres, (4) Mosammat Kulsuma Begum, 0.25 acres, (5) Mr Ashish Chowdhury, 0.20 acres, in total 1.10 acres. It is stated that the whole area of the acquired land under the LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64 was abated by the Tahsilder, Sylhet Municipality Tahsil vide his memo No. 87 dated 27-4-1968. It is stated that it is evident from the register of land acquisition (LA) section that at the request of the director of fisheries E-P, Dhaka vide his letter dated 31-4-64, the possession of an area of 5.59 acres of land covered by Plots. No. 33, 34, 40, 41 and 42 in full, and Plots No. 43 and 44 in parts at Mouza Sylhet Municipality JL No. 91 was handed over to the District Fishery Officer, Sylhet on 28-5-1964 upon requisitioning the same for setting up a Whole Sale Fish Market at Sylhet. 

 10. Thereafter, the property in question was mutated in the name of the Whole Sale Fish Market and respondent No. 6 is paying rent to the government since 1967. It is stated that the aforesaid documents ought to have been placed before the trial Court in TS No. 20 of 1991 but unscrupulous government officers did not come forward to assist the trial Court in adjudicating upon the matter effectively. It is stated that no effort was made by the concerned government officers and employees to establish the fact that without inclusion of 1.10 acres of land in the said Gazette Notification dated 4-3-1965, the total quantum of acquired land does not come to 5.59 acres of land and, thus, non-mentioning of plot No. 41 therein was a mere printing mistake. It is further stated that the said suit was for permanent injunction and the Court has not declared title of the petitioner's predecessors in the said suit and, the title of respondent No. 6 has never been affected. It is stated that since the date of detecting the printing mistake in the Gazette Notification of LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64 regarding non-inclusion of plot No. 41, there were numerous written communication between the BG press and the relevant authority and, finally, the mistake was cured by the impugned Gazette Notification. As such there is no illegality in publishing the same. Hence the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 11. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the respondents cannot claim the case property as acquired property without setting-aside the judgments passed in Title Suit No. 20 of 1991 which has been affirmed by the lower appellate Court, the High Court Division and finally by the Appellate Division. He argues that the impugned Gazette Notification has been published for frustrating the judgments of the highest Court of our jurisdiction. He submits that there are concurrent findings by the trial Court and the appellate Court that the petitioners predecessors are owners in possession of the said plot No. 41 and the same was not published in the Gazette Notification of LA Case No. 7 of 1963-64 and, therefore, this Court sitting in writ jurisdiction is not empowered to question the findings of fact decided finally by the highest Court. He then places "Explanation IV" of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submits that no issue as to the acquisition of plot No. 41 can be raised after the final disposal of the TS No. 20 of 1991 inasmuch as the said "Explanation" prescribes that the issue which was required to be raised as defense but was not raised by the party, would be deemed to have been raised and will be barred by constructive res-judicata. 

 12. In a bid to deal with the issue of non-production of the relevant papers of the LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64 at the trial Court, he places section 114(g) of the Evidence Act and also refers to the case of M Saeed Sehgal vs Kazi Khurshid Hasan 17 DLR (SC) 111, wherein it was held that "plaintiff not calling for the accounts which were available and within his reach, presumption is to be drawn against him". He submits that the said Plot No. 41 cannot be included in the said Gazette Notification dated 4-3-1965 published in connection with under LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64 by a mere amendment of the aforesaid original Gazette Notification inasmuch as the said LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64 was initiated and, finally, ended up under the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1984, and the said Act being dead from the year 1982, inclusion of the said Plot No. 41 in 2010 showing the same as an acquired land under LA Case No 77 of 1963-64 under the said Act is illegal and, on the other hand, the provisions of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 also cannot be applied in publishing the said notice as the case land was not acquired under the Ordinance of 1982. Mr Khalilur Rahman, the learned advocate for the petitioner, then, refers to the case of Osimuddin vs Bangladesh reported in 1 BLC (1996) 375 and, under paragraph 9 of the said judgment, it was held that "in the absence of notification published in the official Gazette as required under sections 4 and 6 of the Forest Act, 1927 the suit land cannot be vested in the Government through Forest Department as the departmental notification cannot affect the right of the public". Thus he submits that since the government did not include Plot No. 41 in the Gazette Notification dated 4-3-1965 finally published in connection with LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64, the right and title of the petitioner's predecessors remained unaffected and their names in SA Khatian No. 1687 remained valid. As such, while they were lawfully owning and possessing the case land upon paying rents/taxes to the government, and they validly transferred the same to the petitioner through other purchases who also got their names mutated in the government record (Annexure A series). 

 15. He next submits that neither respondent No. 7 (land Acquisition Officer) nor respondent No. 4 (Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet) is competent to publish the impugned Gazette Notification. Under the Act of 1948, the government is the only competent authority to publish the Gazette Notification. He submits that the impugned Gazette Notification has been published in violation of Article 42 of the Constitution as well as in contravention of the principles of natural justice inasmuch as no show cause notice was issued or no opportunity of being heard was accorded to the petitioner or his predecessors-in-interest before publication of the impugned amendment circular. 

 18. Per contra, Mr. KM Masud Rumy, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of respondent No. 3 and 4, submits that the impugned Gazette Notification has been published on 28-8-2010 by the competent authority in the public interest which is a bonafide action by the respondents for preservation and protection of valuable government property. He further submits that publication of the impugned Gazette Notification does not violate the petitioner's alleged right under Article 42 of the Constitution and inclusion of Plot No. 41 comprising of an area of 1.10 acres of land cannot be termed as an action vitiated by malice in law. 

 21. He continues to submit that the respondents, under the given circumstances, are now actively considering filing of review petition, though belatedly, before the Appellate Division for reviewing the judgment passed in Title Suit No. 21 of 1991 which was upheld by the appellate Court and, subsequently, by the High Court Division only on the single finding that the government has failed to produce any paper in relation to acquisition of Plot No. 41 and in view of the fact that presently the relevant papers to establish the act of acquisition of the said plot have been available to the office of the Attorney-General, there should not be any difficulty to file review petition given the fraud practiced upon the Courts and it is very highly likely that the review petition may be admitted by the Appellate Division. He finally submits that in view of the fact that the papers relating to the fact of acquisition of Plot No. 41, which ought to have been produced before the trial Court by the government have now surfaced, thus, any one with minimum prudence, in the facts and circumstances of the case, will come to the definite conclusion that due to the connivance of government officials with the plaintiffs of the said suit as well as corrupt practices or, to say the least, poor performance by the Government Pleader engaged in the trial Court for the said suit, the aforesaid papers were deliberately not produced thereby enabling the plaintiffs to obtain a favourable verdict. By not assisting the said Courts in examining the crucial issue of the said suit in its true perspective, the concerned government officers, employees and the Government pleaders practiced fraud upon the trial Court and other Courts. 

 24. The moot question in this writ petition is whether the respondents are empowered to correct the Gazette Notification dated 4-3-1965, which was published in connection with acquisition of a quantum of land of 5.59 acres of plots No. 33, 40, 41, 42 and portion of plots No. 43 and 44 vide LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64. In other words, we are to adjudicate upon the issue as to whether the insertion of plot No. 41 in the Gazette Notification dated 4-3-1965, which was published in connection with the concluded LA Case No 77 of 1963-64, by the impugned amendment circular dated 7-10-2010 is lawful. However, some intricate questions of law, such as application of doctrine of res-judicata, Estoppel, petitioner's protection under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act, are also involved in the adjudication of the present case, which would be dealt with at an appropriate part of this judgment. 

 25. It is an admitted position that the Gazette Notification dated 4-3-1965 mentions plot Nos. 33, 40, 42 and parts of the plot Nos. 43 and 44 but misses plot No. 41. It is also admitted that the total quantum of acquired land is 5.59 acres. Now, by the impugned amendment circular, the said plot No. 41 has been shown as an acquired plot under LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64, Gazette of which was published on 4-3-1965 though it has finally been adjudicated upon by the competent Courts that plot No. 41 has never been acquired. Thus, the present writ petition involves a two-fold Situation. 

 26. Scenario No. 1 in the instant writ petition is that in LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64, plot No. 41 was acquired but the same was inadvertently not published in the Gazette Notification dated 4-3-1965. In order to adjudicate upon the above scenario, this Court's task will be only to examine and asses the legality or validity of the publication of the impugned amendment circular dated 7-10-2010 (Annexure-E) and, in that evident, this Court is required to see whether plot No. 41 was at all acquired by LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64. 

 30. To attach the instant writ petition with the "Scenario No. 2", the competency of this Court in making any findings on the issue of acquisition of plot No. 41, which has been finally adjudicated upon by the competent Courts, becomes pertinent. As it is a settled principle of the law that writ Court is not an appellate Court and, thus, it cannot get engaged in appreciation of the evidences and examine the correctness of the finding arrived at by the trial Court, we, notwithstanding the aforesaid position of the law, would undertake the task of going through the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court in Title Suit No. 20 of 1991 for the reasons to be stated at the last part of this judgment. 

 31. It appears that the suit was for permanent injunction, which was filed in the early part of the year 1991 and decreed on 18-11-91. It further appears that the father of Rajani Ranjan Gupta was the original owner of the suit land and it was the case of the plaintiffs of the aforesaid suit that Rajani Ranjan Gupta entered into an agreement in the middle of the year of 1982 to sell the suit land and, accordingly, the said Rajani Ranjan Gupta, upon taking the earnest money from the plaintiffs and receiving required income tax certificate, gave delivery of possession of the suit land to the plaintiffs and the registration of the suit land was agreed to be executed after receiving the remaining amount which he could not do due to his death. Then, the sole son of Rajani Ranjan Gupta, Rakkhani Ranjan Gupta executed the said registration of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs, who, upon mutating their respective names therein, became the owners and possessors of the suit land. The cause of action of the said suit arose when the plaintiffs cultivation of the land in question was halted by the District Fishery Office in the month of Agrahayan of 1397 BS, as appears from the judgment and decree dated 18-11-1991 passed in Title Suit No. 20 of 1991, though from the averments of the instant writ petition it transpires that the suit was instituted when the said office mutated its name behind the back of the plaintiffs upon opening Khatian No. 7640. 

 33. The case of defendant No. 2 (Government of Bangladesh) was that the Government acquired 5.59 acres of land, consisting of Plots Nos. 33, 41, 42 and the parts of the plot Nos. 43 and 44 under the Mouza of No. 1 Municipality appertaining to Khatian No. 9687 for setting up the "Whole Sale Fish Market at Sylhet" vide LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64 and the said lands were handed over to District Fishery Officer on 18-5-64. 

 48. In the light of the provisions of law as provided in section 44 of the Evidence Act as well as the settled principle laid down by our Apex Court in a number of cases that fraud vitiates every right, be that a legal or vested right, our view, in line with the aforesaid provisions of law and principle, is that whatever the right may have accrued by the petitioner, if the government can prove through a competent Court that fraud has been practiced upon the trial Court in obtaining the judgment and decree of the TS No. 20 of 91, the procedural law like res-judicata or shield like estoppel are hardly able to defend the petitioner inasmuch the said doctrine or principles are not capable to stand in the way of granting justice by a competent Court when the fact of practicing fraud upon the Courts will be proved and established before the said competent Court. In the case of Begum Khaleda Zia vs Government of Bangladesh 63 DLR 385, the plea of estoppel, waiver and acquisance could not stand in the way though the petitioner, upon mutating her name, was owning and possessing the land for 28 years without facing any hindrance from any corner. Therefore, the performance demonstrated by a group of unscrupulous government officers or employees cannot be said to be the true "representative" (wording from section 115 of the Evidence Act ushering the concept of Estoppel) in a litigation where public property and interest is involved and, as such, the subsequent bonafide step (declaration, act or omission) by another group of government officials with patriotic zeal should be taken into consideration. In the case of People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Most Sharifian Bibi 43 DLR (AD) 112, the RS Khatian was prepared in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor who paid rent to the government and the plaintiff subsequently, upon mutating its name, also paid rent to the government, nonetheless, the Appellate Division discarded the application of doctrine of Estoppel. 

 58. From the above discussions and observations, this Court is led to hold that in spite of detecting the fact of practicing fraud upon the Courts in obtaining the judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 20 of 91, the same being not set-aside by a competent Court and, thus, being in operation as of now, the hands of this Court are tight and not well equipped to discharge the instant Rule. Consequently, the impugned "Amendment Circular" being নং জে প্র সি/এল, এ/ ৪৪৭(৩)dated 28-8-2010 published in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 7-10-2010 (Annexure-E) appears to be without any arms to protect it for now and, accordingly, the same is declared to have been published without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 66. So far my reasoning’s are concerned, my looking at the matter is from the angle that the Rule in this writ petition has been issued upon the respondents "to show cause as to why the amendment circular being JaPro C/LA/ 447(3) 'dated 7-10-2010 (Annexure-E) issued under the signature of Respondent No. 7, Land Acquisition Officer, Syhlet by inclusion of the petitioner's land as described in the schedule to the writ petition as Acquisitioned land of LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64 shall not be declared to have been published without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect, "From the aforesaid terms of the Rule it appears that the whole question encircles as to whether the publication of the impugned amendment circular (Annexure-E) was in accordance with law. To answer the query and to come to a conclusion of this point in issue we need to see firstly; as to who issued the impugned amendment circular, Annexure E and whether he had/has the authority to issue such circular under section 5(7) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948; and secondly: if the same is for the purpose of amending/correcting the original circular dated 4-3-1965 then whether the same has been issued or published by the appropriate authority and whether the same can be done after 45 years of final publication of the same in the Gazette under section 5(7) of the said Act 1948, when the said law has been repealed by section 1(3) and (4) read with sections 16 and 17 of the said Act itself. 

 67. The background of the case is, admittedly, Rajani Ranjan Gupta was the CS recorded tenant of CS Plot No. 41 covering an area of 1.10 acres of land whose name was rightly recorded and published in SA Khatian No. 1687 in 1962; after his death his son Rakkhini Ranjan Gupta became the owner of the said property. On the other hand, it is alleged by the respondents that in LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64, the entire 1.10 acres of land in Plot No. 41, along with the entire land of CS Plots Nos. 33, 40 and 42 and parts of Plots Nos. 43 and 44 total 5.59 acres of land were acquired by the authority which was published finally in the Dhaka Gazette on 4-3-1965. It is also admitted that Abdus Sahid and others claimed to be the owners of the entire 1.10 acres of land in Plot No. 41 by purchase from Rakkhani Ranjan Gupta, son of Rajani Ranjan Gupta by five deeds of sale all in 1990 whereupon, they got their names mutated in place of Rajani Ranjan Gupta and enjoying the same by paying rents to the government in their respective names. In 1991 when the District fishery officer, Sylhet, threatened them to dispossess from the said land on the plea that the property is an acquired property, they filed Title Suit No. 20 of 1991, for permanent injunction, against the District Fisheries Officer, Subid Bazar, Syhlet and Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner Sylhet. It is also admitted that the said two defendants contested the suit by filing written statement contending intralia that entire 1.10 acres of land of Plot No. 41 along with full Plots Nos. 33, 40 and 42 and parts of Plots No. 43 and 44, total 5.59 acres of land, are acquired property and the District Fisheries Office is in possession of the same by way of possession handing over certificate dated 28-5-1964, Ext 'Ka' (Annexure A-I to the affidavit in opposition filed by Respondent No. 3). It is further admitted that the said suit was finally decreed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sylhet, by his judgment and decree dated 28-11-1991 holding that on the face of nonproduction of the records of LA case No. 77 of 1963-64; and on the face of plaintiffs' registered title documents, Mutation Khatian and the proof of possession through payment of land revenue taxes to the government by rent receipts; and on the face of all the evidences, both oral and documentary, of the plaintiffs proving their possession; and on the face of Abdun Noor, the alleged bargadar of the District Fisheries Office, being not produced and examined to prove possession of District Fisheries Office; and in the absence of any pleading as to non-mentioning Plot No. 41 in the finally published gazette dated 4-3-1965 was erroneous or due to mistake the said Plot No. 41 was not mentioned in the said gazettee dated 4-3-1965 as to final acquisition; and also on the face of advocate commissioner's report which concurrently proved plaintiffs' possession in the said Plot No. 41, even after being cross examined by the defendants, the learned Assistant Judge held that 'the plaintiffs have been able to prove their prima facie title in the 1.10 acres of land of Plot No. 41 and also having successfully proved their exclusive possession in the suit land both by oral and documentary evidences and also through the Advocate Commissioners' report and accordingly decreed the suit and the defendants were permanently restrained by an order of injunction from dispossessing the plaintiffs from the said land in Plot No. 41. It is also admitted that the said decree was affirmed in Title Appeal No. 6 of 1992, preferred by the aforesaid two defendants who then unsuccessfully moved the High Court Division and also the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in Civil Revision No. 4627 of 2004 and CPLA No. 2041 of 2008 respectively. Thus the findings and decision of the learned Assistant Judge in Title Suit No. 20 of 1991 is a valid judgment which is still in operation. After the appeal in the Appellate Division was dismissed on 4-5-2009 the present respondents published the impugned amendment circular on 7-10-2010. Hence this Rule. 

 68. With this backdrop this writ petition has been taken up for hearing and my brother in his judgment made the Rule absolute with observations and directions as mentioned earlier. My anxiety is when the law provides that with the final publication in the Gazette Notification the entire acquisition process ends and when the gazette notification was published in 1965 without incorporating Plot No. 41 and when the law, under which the acquisition was made, has been repealed, whether the said gazette of 1965 can be rectified by the impugned amendment circular dated 7-10-2010 after unsuccessful exercise up to the Appellate Division and after the law being repealed , on the plea of mistake and of course behind the back of the plaintiffs or the writ petitioner, the subsequent transferees. If we, at all, take it as a mistake then question arises whether the said mistake can be rectified after final publication in the gazette in 1965 and whether the land acquisition officer, Sylhet, has any authority to publish the said impugned amendment circular, whereby he tried to include Plot No. 41 in the Gazette Notification of 1965. In this respect we need to see section 5 of the Act of 1948 which deals with final publication. The same reads is as follows: 

 (7) The Government shall then publish in the Official Gazette a notice to the effect that the Government has decided to acquire the requisitioned property. On and from the beginning of the day on which the notice is so published the requisitioned property vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and the period of such requisition of such property shall end." 

 69. Having gone through the aforesaid provision of law it appears that it is the "government" who, as it thinks fit, may acquire any requisitioned property, on the proposal of the Deputy Commissioner in the manner as provided thereafter. Interestingly, sub section (la) to subsection (5) of section 5 of the Act of 1948 deals with the power of the Deputy Commissioner to deal with the matters relating up to proposal for and report regarding acquisition. Whereas sub section (6) and (7) thereof, empowers the "government" only to finalize the acquisition upon considering the report of the Deputy Commissioner and thereby finally publish the same in the Gazette which accordingly brings the entire proceedings of requisition and acquisition to an end upon absolute vesting of the said property in the government free from all encumbrances on and from the date of publication of the gazette notification. One thing is required to be bear in mind that after the gazette notification the requisition or acquisition of the property comes to an end which means it becomes a 4 past and closed transaction, empowering no-one to make any amendment or correction of the same. If, for argument sake, it is taken that non-inclusion of any plot/property in the finally published gazette notification was a mistake, which is of course not the case of the respondents in the civil suit, even then the correction, if any, is to be made or allowed under the law, by the government not by the Land Acquisition Officer, who being a subordinate officer to the Deputy Commissioner, under no circumstances can be treated as the "government". Although Act of 1948 did not define the word 'government' but reading section-2 of the said Act, as a whole it appears that the government is someone else other than the Deputy Commissioner or Additional Deputy Commissioner, Joint Deputy Commissioner and Assistant Commissioner or [Deputy Magistrate and Deputy Collector] authorized by the Deputy Commissioner to exercise any power conferred, or perform any duty imposed, on the Deputy Commissioner by or under the said Act. The Land Acquisition Officer being subordinate to the Deputy Com-missioner, does not have any authority to correct the gazette notification published by the government in 1965. In this respect we can also take the assistance of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Rules, 1948 wherein, though government has not been defined like the Act, but the forms printed for the purpose of issuance of notice under section 3, namely, requisition or under section 5 (1) and 5 (3) namely, intention of the government to acquire a property or filing of objection, if any, to requisition of a property, or claim for compensation; and also if we see Form D which is for the purpose of issuing notice under section 5(7) for final acquisition of a property, we find that form A to C are used for notices to be issued under section 3, 5(1) and 5(3), respectively, which shows that those are to be issued/published under the signature of the "Deputy Commissioner" or "Additional Deputy Commissioner." Interestingly, the notice under form D, which is for the purpose of final acquisition of a property to be issued under section 5(7) is required to be published under the signature of the "Secretary/ Deputy Secretary" "by Order of the President". So, if we take into consideration the provision of section 21 of the General Clauses Act then we find that the authority which can pass order it can vary, after, amend or rescind that order. In the present case when the final notice was published by the "Government" under section 5(7) of the Act of 1948 meaning "by order of the President" under the signature of Secretary or Deputy Secretary it is only the Government not the Land Acquision officer who has the authority to amend or correct the said gazette notification not the "Land Acquisition Officer" as has been done in the present case as appears from the impugned Annexure-E to the writ petition. 

 70. On the other hand when the Act of 1948 was given a longevity up to 34 (thirty four) years from the date of its effect i.e. from 16-8-1948 (under section 1(3) and 1(4) of the said Act) meaning the longevity of the said law was till 15-8-1982. With the end of 15-8-1982 the said (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 had its natural death and under section 16 of the said Act it has been provided that 'on the expiry of this Act, the provisions of section 8 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 shall apply, as if this Act has been repealed by an Act of the Legislature'. So the law which had its natural death, pursuant to section 1(3) and 1(4) read with section 16 of the Act of 1948 and thereafter when the new law namely the "Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982" came into operation and there being no saving clause provided for in either of the two laws to protect the acts and deeds or anything made under Act of 1948, the authority, not to speak of the Land Acquisition Officer, under no circumstances had any power to amend or correct the finally published Gazette Notification of 1965 by the impugned amendment circular, Annexure E. 

 71. On the other hand, when the District Fisheries Office or the Deputy Commissioner, Syhlet, did not produce anything to prove that the property was requisitioned property and subsequently was acquired, by producing any piece of paper nor admitted in the suit that mistakenly the same was not published in the gazette of 1965 and accordingly having lost in all the courts up to the Appellate Division, the respondents, under no circumstances, now can issue such impugned amendment circular on the plea that mistakenly the said plot was not incorporated in the gazette of 1965. This is nothing but sheer Latches on the part of the Respondents and, as such, they cannot take advantage of their own laches. Thus publication of the impugned amendment circular after 45 years from the final publication of Gazette Notification or 20 years from the institution of the suit under no circumstances can be termed as a bonafide action on the part of the respondents. Moreover, when by virtue of decree dated 28-11-1991 the plaintiffs' possession have been affirmed and subsequently the writ petitioner having purchased the same from the plaintiffs after the dismissal of the CPLA by the Appellate Division the writ petition is a bonafide purchaser with value and notice of the contested decree as well as the government records and having mutated its name with the government offices and is paying land development taxes to the government the publication of the impugned amendment circular in the gazette (Annexure E), without serving any notice upon the petitioner or its predecessors, is nothing but an arbitrary action of the respondents which proves their high handedness whereby the judgment and decree affirmed up to the Appellate Division has tried to be made frustrated. Such arbitrary action of the respondents has also violated the principle of natural justice of being heard. 

 72. Thus the respondents having failed to prove the acquisition of the disputed land in the finally published Gazette Notification of 1965 up to the Appellate Division on contest and the predecessors in interest of the petitioner having got their names mutated and recorded in the government record as evident from Annexure A and A (1) series, and the petitioner having got its name also mutated vide Mutation case No. 4214/10-11 after the purchase as evident from Annexures C-3 , the petitioner is a bonafide purchaser with notice on payment of adequate value, as such the respondents, under no circumstances have any authority to issue the impugned amendment circular (Annexure-E) without notifying the petitioner. 

 73. Since the subject matter of the Rule is 'whether the impugned amendment circular inserting Plot No. 41 in the Gazette Notification of 1965 in connection with LA Case No. 77 of 1963-64 is proper and since I have come to a conclusion that the said publication of Gazette Notification of 1965 was the finality of the requisition/acquisition proceeding, the correction of the said gazette of 1965 by the impugned amendment circular (Annexure E) published by the land Acquisition Officer, Sylhet after more than 45 years without having any authority of such publication, the impugned circular (Annexure E) thus is without lawful authority as stated hereinabove and since the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 20 of 1991 is not the subject matter of this Rule rather the same has been produced as an Annexure to prove that how the respondents miserably failed to prove any title and possession on the said piece of land, I have got no other option but to constrain myself to remain within the discussion as to the legality of the publication of the impugned Gazette Notification not anything beyond that. Under the present context we cannot extend ourselves to scan the judgment passed in Title Suit No. 20 of 1991 or in the appeal/revision arose out of the same. Moreover, till the said decree is in force and not set-aside by a competent court, the impugned amendment circular, published after leasing the case up to the Appellate Division, shall have no bearing other than Creating chaos and confusion in the mind of the Public. Our jurisdiction being limited within Article 102 of the Constitution we are not empowered to sit as an appellate court to see the validity of the said judgment and the same being not the subject matter of this Rule any observation/finding on the same is nothing but at best be an academic discussion which the Appellate Division directed all to refrain from as has been held in the case of Abdul Mannan Khan vs Bangladesh reported in 64 DLR (AD) 169 that 'while deciding a case, a Court shall not embark upon unnecessary academic discussions and shall confine itself within the issues, which will crop up from the pleadings of the respective parties.' Here in the present case decree of Title Suit No. 20 of 1991 being not the subject matter in issue we are not empowered to see the validity of the same not we can make any observation as to genuinenity of the same and accordingly direct anybody to investigate into the matter. 

 75. Hence, the Rule is made absolute and, the impugned amendment Circular being No. JaPro C/LA/447(3) dated 7-10-2010 (Annexure-E) issued under the signature of Respondent No. 7, Land Acquisition Officer, Sylhet whereby the petitioner's 1.10 acres of land in CS Plot No. 41, fully described in the schedule to the writ petition, as acquisitioned land of LA Case No. 77/63-64 is hereby declared to have been published illegally, without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

2. The short facts for disposal of the role are that the land originally belonged to Joy Chandra Banta and R.S. Khatian in respect thereof was correctly prepared and finally published in his favour. Joy Chandra Barua transferred the suit schedule-I land in favour of Mohan Banshi Banta by a registered Kabala and accordingly delivered possession of the same. Mohan Banshi Barua by a registered kabala dated 14.10.1969 transferred the suit schedule-I land in favour of Hamangshu Barua who subsequently transferred the same in favour of Sneha Bala Barua mother of the plaintiffs by a registered kabala dated 10.3.1970 and accordingly delivered possession of suit schedule-1 land in her 'favour. After purchasing the schedule-1 land Sneha Bala Banta constructed a dwelling house on the suit schedule-1 land and had been possessing the same with her family members; that being satisfied by the nursing of the of the plaintiff No. 1 Sneha Bala Barua transferred .02 acres of land out of suit schedule-I land to the plaintiff No. I by a registered deed of gift dated 28.12.1987 and accordingly delivered possession of the same in favour of the plaintiff No.1 and the plaintiff No.1 has been possessing the some giving specific boundaries. Sneha Bala Barua died on 19.1.1993 and as such the plaintiffs became owners in possession of rest .02 acres of land by inheritance. The Plaintiff No.1 by amicable arrangement with his brothers and sisters became owner in possession of the entire suit schedule I land and have been possessing the same on payment of rent till to-day. The defendant No.1 claimed suit schedule 1(Ka)land for the first time at the last part of November 1997 which is the part of schedule I land and in collusion with defendants 2 and 3 gave out open threat to the plaintiffs that they would take possession of the suit schedule- bka) land by evicting the plaintiffs there from by force. On enquiry plaintiffs came to know that the defendant No I has created a deed of gift dated 19.6.1991 in respect of the suit land alleged to be executed by the mother of the plaintiffs in his favour. Sneha Bala Barua mother of the plaintiffs did not execute any such kabala in respect of the suit land in favour of the defendant No.1. The alleged registered deed of gift dated 19.6.1991 is false, fraudulent, collusive without consideration and void and mother of plaintiffs did not execute the said deed in favour of defendant No. l. Plaintiffs have been possessing land of schedule 1 (ka) in which they acquired right and title by inheritance from their mother and defendants have acquired no right and title in suit schedule 1(ka) land by the alleged deed of gift dated 19.6.1991. As the defendants gave out open threat to the plaintiffs on 18.1.1999 for taking forcible possession of the suit land and as the alleged deed of gift dated 19.6.1991 has created clouds in the right, title, interest and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land plaintiffs were compelled to file the suit with the prayer for the reliefs slated above. 

 3. Defendants No. 1-3 contested the suit by filing a written statements denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and after taking all the preliminary objection as to maintainability of the suit it is their respective case that the suit land originally belonged to Joy Chandra Barua in whose name R.S. Khatian was correctly prepared and finally published; Joy Chandra Barua transferred the suit schedule 1 land in favour of Mohan Banashi Barua by a registered Kabala and Mohan Banshi Banta while in possession of the suit schedule-I land transferred the same to Himangshu Banta and subsequently Himangshu transferred .04 acres of land to Sneha Bala by registered Kabala dated 10.03.1970 and accordingly delivered possession to her. Sneha Bala Banta gifted .02 acres of land out of P4 acres to the plaintiff No.1 by a registered deed of gift dated 28.12.1987 and the rest .02 acres of land was transferred by Sneha Bala Barua by a registered deed of gift dated 19.06.1991 in favour of defendant No.1. Plaintiff No.1 and defendant No.I Acquired .02 acres of land each by the above said two registered deeds of gift dated 28.12.1987 and 19.06.1991. Defendant No.1 has been possessing the land described in schedule I(ka) of the plaint and on the other hand plaintiff No.1 has been possessing the rest .02 sataks which is adjacent to the land of schedule I (ha) land. Plaintiff never possessed or ever claimed the land described in schedule I (ka) land of the plaint. It is a down right falsehood to say that defendants gave out open threat to plaintiffs on 18.01.1998 to dispossess them from the suit land as alleged in the plaint and as such there is no cause of action for filing the suit. Deed of gift dated 19.1K,I991 executed by Sneha Bab in of defendant No.1 is a genuine and on the basis of the same defendant No.1 has been possessing the suit schedule l(ka) land, plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit schedule I (ka) land and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 8. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that, the Court of appeal below wholly misconceived the issues involved in the suit and the relevant law applicable thereto and in consequence erred in law resulting in an error in the decision in decreeing the suit. The learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner further submits that having regard to the established principle that if a person alleges that a particular transaction is false, fraudulent, collusive and void the burden is on that person to prove the allegation and having regard to the pleading of the plaintiffs in the suit and evidence adduced by them in support of their case learned Additional District Judge committed a grave error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in not dismissing the appeal upon a finding that the plaintiffs singularly failed to discharge the burden on them in this regard. The learned Advocate also submits that the learned Additional District Judge framed five issues for deciding the appeal and committed mistakes and illegalities in deciding issue Nos. 3-5 together and so doing jumbled up the subject matter of the suit thereby could not le and decide the case of the parties from their proper angle of vision and perspective and made a mess of whole thing in deciding the issue, learned District Judge therefore committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that the learned Additional District Judge committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in setting aside the judgment of the learned Assistant Judge without noticing and reversing the findings of the learned Assistant Judge the Court of appeal below failed to read and appreciate the oral and documentary evidence of the parties on the question of the plaintiffs knowledge of alleged disputed Kabala dated 19.6.1991 and therefore, apparently committed an error in disturbing the finding of the Trial Court in this point in as much as the findings of the Trial Court is based on proper reading and appreciation of the oral evidence adduced by the parties, the judgment of reversal in this case is neither legal nor proper. The learned Advocate also submits that there is error apparent in the judgment of the Court of appeal below in that the Court of Appeal below reversed the positive finding of the Trial Court on the point as to the possession of the suit property without assigning any cogent reason therefore and even without referring to the oral evidence on record on the question and thus the Appellate Court below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Counsel for the petitioner then submits that the genuineness of the registered deed of gift dated 19.6.1991 executed by Sneha Bala Banta has been questioned in the plaint by the plaintiff and therefore the onus of proving the plaint case lies upon the plaintiff opposite parties. The learned Additional District Judge committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in allowing the appeal selling aside the judgment and decree of the Trial Court upon a finding that the learned Assistant Judge should have sent the disputed deed of gift dated 19.6.1991 before Hand Writing Expert for opinion by examination and comparison of the L.T.I. of Sneha Bala appearing in the deed of gift with those admitted signature and L.T.Is. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner again submits that the learned Assistant Judge found that Sneha Bala gifted .02 acres of land to the plaintiff  Deizi Banta & Ors M.K.M. Shohidul litta,J1465 no.I by a registered deed of gift dated 28.12.1987 and subsequently she again transferred the rest .02 acres of land to the defendant no. 1 by registered deed of gift dated 19.6.1991 which has been challenged by the plaintiffs in the instant suit, the above said two registered deed of gills were written by the same scribe the. L.T.I. of Sneha Bala apparent on both the deeds have been indentified by the same person namely. Prabodh Ranjan Banta and the attesting witnesses of both the documents are the same. Probodh Ranjan Banta was examined and cross examined as D.W.3 who proved execution of both the deeds by Sneha Bala. The learned Additional District Judge without considering the above aspects decreed the suit upon a finding that the Trial Court should have sent the disputed deed of gift for experts opinion and thus the learned Additional District Judge is totally misdirected in passing such erroneous finding and committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice as such as the learned Assistant Judge is quite competent under Section 73 of the Evidence Act to compare the L.T.I. of the executants Sneha Bala appearing in the aforesaid deed of gift dated 19.6.1991 with her other L.T.I.'s available in the record of the suit such as admitted registered deed of gift dated 28.12.1987. The learned Counsel for the petitioner further submits that the appellate Court below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in not dismissing the suit upon a finding that the.suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner also submits that the learned Additional District Judge decreed the suit declaring the deed of gift dated 19.6.1991 is collusive and void upon an erroneous finding based on surmise and conjecture that though the defendant no.1 got the disputed land by a registered deed of gift dated 19.6.1991 executed by Sneha Bala but he neither mutated his name in the khatian by filling a Mutation case nor he paid rent of the disputed land in as much as Mutation Khatian and the rent receipts are not the documents of title. The learned Advocate for the petitioner lastly submits that the defendant petitioners became owners in possession of the suit land on the strength of a registered deed of gift dated 19.9.1991, the impugned judgment and -decree dated 29.3.2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge. 755 Court Chittagong in other Appeal No.235 of 1999 is erroneous.

2. That on 25-2-81 the petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 276 of 981 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka (transferred to 4th Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat renumbered as Title Suit No. 244 of 1992) for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of the following land of Schedule 'A' comprising of an area of 0.1256 acres of land out of the land of CS Plot Nos. 88 and 107 corresponding to SA Plot Nos. 62 and 12 corresponding to RS Plot No. 557 of Mouza Old Tejkunipara, JL No. 80 now Tejgaon, JL No. 3, PS Tejgaon, District Dhaka recorded in CS Khatian No. 175 corresponding to SA Khatian Nos. 43 and 13 corresponding to RS DP Khatian No. 301 butted and bounded by: 

 An area of more or less 2 kathas equivalent to 0.0330 acres of land being part of CS Plot No. 107 corresponding to SA Plot No.12 corresponding to RS Plot No. 557 now wrongly included in RS Plot No. 556 of Mouza Old Tejkunipara, JL No. 89, now Tejkunipara, JL No. 5, recorded in CS Khatian No.175 corresponding to SA Khatian No.13 corresponding to RS DP Khatian No. 301 marked 'X' in the hand sketch map and butted and bounded by: 

 3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that the land of CS Khatian No. 175 of Mouza Tejkunipara, PS Tejgaon, District Dhaka originally belonged to 2 brothers, Fazar Ali Sheikh and Mabu Sheikh alias Nabu Sheikh. That for convenience of the possession, the said two brothers namely, Fazar Ali and Mabu, amicably partitioned their entire property before CS operation. By such amicable partition, the lands of CS Plot Nos. 87, 107 and 120 were given in the Saham of Mabu Sheikh and the lands of CS Plot Nos. 88, 106, 108, 118 and 416 were given in the Saham of Fazar Ali Sheikh. Accordingly, during CS operation the lands of CS Plot Nos. 87,107 and 120 were shown in the possession of Mabu Sheikh in the column provided for recording possession and the lands of CS Plot Nos. 88, 106, 108, 118 and 416 were shown in possession of said Fazar Ali Sheikh and the record was finally published accordingly. That the said Fazar Ali Sheikh while in exclusive possession of the land of CS Plot Nos.88 and other plots referred to above, died leaving one son Abdul Jabbar as his legal heir and successor. The said Abdul Jabbar sold different portions of CS Plot No. 88 to different people for valuable consideration and put the purchasers into possession within specific block. The said Abdul Jabbar sold an area of ten kathas equivalent to 0.1650 acres of land to one Sirajul Islam, son of Hajee Abdul Ghani Mal for valuable consideration by a registered Kabala No. 3017 dated 6-3-56 registered in the office of Sadar Sub-Registrar, Dhaka, and put the said Sirajul Islam into possession of the land sold to him within specific boundary. The said Sirajul Islam possessed his purchased land for some years and then sold to different people. The said Sirajul Islam sold an area of 4½ (four and half) khatas equivalent to 0.0750 acres of land out of his purchased ten khatas equivalent to 0.1650 acres of land out of the land of CS Plot No. 88 to the plaintiff No. 2 for valuable consideration by a registered kabala dated 14th Ashar, 1373 BS corresponding to 29-6-66 and put the plaintiff No. 2 into possession of the said 0.0750 acres of land within the following boundary: 

 That during SA operation the land of CS Plot No. 88 was changed to SA Plot No. 62 and recorded as SA Plot No. 62 and SA Khatian No. 43 and the land of CS Plot No. 107 was changed to SA plot No. 12 for an area of 0.54 acres of land and recorded in SA Khatian No. 13 of Mouza Tejkunipara and the SA Khatians were finally published. The plaintiff No. 2 after her purchase of 4½ kathas of land out of the land of CS Plot No. 88 corresponding to SA Plot No. 62 got her name mutated and jama was separated from the Government acquired estate vide MS Case No.1114 (SG) 74-75 dated 12-9-75 from the office of CO (Rev), Tejgaon and paid rent separately. Similarly the plaintiff No.1 also after his purchase of 3 kathas 2 chataks of land out of the land of CS Plot No.107 corresponding to SA Plot No.12 got his name mutated and jama was separated from the Government acquired estate and paid the rent to the Government separately. That the plaintiff No.1 is the husband of the plaintiff No.2, they for the convenience of possession and enjoyment, amalgamated their purchased lands and surrounded the same by distinct boundary marks. The plaintiffs constructed three-storied building in the purchased portion of CS Plot No. 88 by obtaining plan approved by DIT and they kept the portion of CS Plot No.107 vacant within the same boundary, the same was duly recorded in the names of plaintiffs as against which the defendant filed an objection case under Rule 30 of the EBT Rules and managed to obtain a favourable order, against which the plaintiff filed an appeal No. 28471 of 1979 under Rule 31 of the said Rules. That during the pendency of the said appeal, the defendant trespassed into the suit land and thereby dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land on the 10th Poush, 1385 BS which compelled the plaintiffs to file the instant suit. 

 4. That the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 as defendant Nos.1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter alia, that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 purchased 9-1/8 decimals of land in the south eastern part of CS Plot No.107 of CS Khatian No. 175 (contiguous to western part of CS Plot No. 106) from Abdul Jabbar Mia, son of Fazar Ali Sheikh, original CS recorded tenant by kabala dated 7-12-62 and 10-12-62 and has been in possession of the said purchased land by erecting boundary wall and constructing semi-pucca house thereon. That the plaintiff No.1 purchased in the name of plaintiff No. 2 some land from CS Plot No. 88 (which is contiguous to CS Plot No.106), that as there was no road to enter into the land purchased by the plaintiff, the plaintiff requested the defendant No.1 and local influential person for making arrangements of a road. According to the request of the plaintiff No.1, the Matabbars of the locality took initiative to construct 12 feet wide road. That the local members namely, Mahabubur Rahman Goraha, Md Ali Akbar, Md Abdul Majid, Md Omar Ali, Golam Mohiuddin, Abdur Rashid and Abdur Motaleb took decisions : 

 8. The learned Counsel Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr Anwarul Azim Khair, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner, submits that both the Courts below were absolutely wrong and erroneous in dismissing the case of the plaintiff. Both the Courts below, without applying their judicial mind and without proper assessment of the evidence on record, came to a wrong and erroneous finding in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff. The learned Counsel further submits that it is a suit for declaration with a prayer for recovery of khas possession. Admittedly, the plaintiff No. 2 purchased 4½ kathas of land on 29-6-66 in CS Plot No.88 and subsequently plaintiff No.1 purchased 3 kathas and 2 chataks of land by a registered kabala dated 4-4-1969 from Abdul Majid in CS Plot No.107. The plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 are husband and wife. On the other hand, the defendant purchased 5½ kathas of land in CS Plot No.106. The suit land is situated in CS Plot No.107 comprising 2 kathas and 1 chatak of land out of 3 kathas and 1 chatak of land purchased on the basis of sale deed dated 4-4-69. Admittedly, the title deed is in the name of the plaintiff. The defendant claimed the suit land comprising 2 kathas and 1 chatak which was decided to be transferred in the name of the defendant in a Salish in exchange of 9 x 70 square feet of land in CS Plot No. 106 which belonged to the defendant for constructing a 12 ft. road to go to the house of the plaintiff. The learned Counsel next submits that the basis of the claim of the defendants over the suit land was the so-called Salishnama of exchange executed on 6-6-68. When the defendants managed to record the suit land in CS Khatian No. 107 against which, an appeal under Rule 31 of EBT was pending, at that time their names and the defendants on 10th Poush, 1385 BS forcibly entered into the suit land and dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land. Both the Courts below, ignoring the legal implication of exchange under section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act came to a wrong and fallacious decision in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff. The section provides that, a transfer of property in completion of an exchange can be made only in the manner provided for the transfer of such property by sale. The learned Counsel also submits that the plaintiff in his deposition, categorically denied that he did not put his signature in the so-called Salishnama to exchange the property of the plaintiff. Since transfer of property by exchange can be made only in the manner provided for transfer of property by sale in the eye of law, the Salishnama has got no legal bearing unless it is a registered instrument. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act defined sale as under: "Sale how made Such transfer, in the case of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred (Taka) and upwards, or in the case of a reversion or other intangible thing, can be made only by a registered instrument." Now, in the absence of any registered deed of exchange in pursuance of the so-called Salishnama, it is absolutely an inoperative document which is denied by the plaintiff. The learned Counsel further submits that both the Courts below committed an error of law in not taking into consideration the legal implication of section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act and acted illegally in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff. The defendant did not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit property because in pursuance of the so-called Salishnama no deed of exchange was actually executed and registered. The observation made by the Courts below that the plaintiff has got no right, title and interest in the suit property is absolutely wrong and perverse, even the defendant did not challenged the title of the plaintiff and if the defendant challenged the title of the plaintiff, in that case there can be no execution of the exchange of deed because unless two persons mutually agree to transfer the ownership of one thing and ownership of another, there can be no exchange according to the definition of exchange under section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act. Rather, the defendant did not acquire any right, title and interest by the so-called Salishnama in the suit property. The learned Courts below did not arrive at any finding that the defendant actually handed over the possession of 9 x 70 square feet of land from CS Plot No. 106 in exchange of the suit land. Admittedly, the defendant purchased 5½ kathas of land in CS Plot No. 106 but an Advocate Commissioner was appointed by the Court at the instance of the plaintiff for measurement of the suit land and also the land of the defendant in CS Plot No. 106, who submitted a report that the defendant's land comprising of 5½ kathas remained intact. Therefore, the assertion made by the defendant and observed by the Courts below that the defendant handed over the possession of 9 x 70 square feet of land from CS Plot No. 106 in exchange of the suit land proved to be false. Finally, the learned Counsel submits that the Courts below did not at all discuss anything about the evidence of Advocate Commissioner and his report. The learned Courts below without consideration of the material evidence on record i.e the Advocate Commissioner's report affecting the merit of the case came to a wrong and fallacious finding in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff which is liable to be interfered by this Court and hence the Rule should be made absolute. 

 9. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr Abdul Quaiyum with Mr Sasti Sarker, appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite parties, submits that the concurrent finding of the facts cannot be disturbed in revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Counsel further submits that in furtherance of a Salish, a common fund was raised to purchase the suit land from Abdul Majid. But the plaintiff, taking advantage of the deed in his name, subsequently denied to execute the exchange deed. Next, he submits that both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff was not dispossessed from the suit land. The learned Counsel finally submits that the judgment of affirmance is generally immune to be assailed unless it is vitiated by misreading and non-consideration of the material evidence on record. In the instant suit, there is no misreading and non-consideration, as such no interference is called for in revision by this Court hence, the Rule should be discharged. 

 "If there is misreading of evidence and non-consideration of some material evidence then it was incumbent on the revisional Court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case."

2. The case of the appellants, in brief, is that the pre-emptor-appellants filed pre-emption Case No. 8 of 1996 in the Court of the Additional Senior Assistant Judge, Mymensingh under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1948 for pre-emption of 12-1/3 acres of land against the pre-emptee-respondent on the allegation, inter alia, that 14 acres of land of ROR Plot No. 274 appertaining to S.A. Khatian No. 131 was recorded in the name of Md. Shahed Ali who died leaving behind the pre-emptor-petitioners, Md. Shahidul Islam and others as heirs; that the pre-emptor Nos.1, 2 and 3 are the 2nd wife, a son and a daughter respectively of the said Md. Shahed Ali respectively and the said Md. Shahidul Islam is a son of the said Md. Shahed Ali; that by amicable partition amongst the heirs of the said Md. Shahed Ali, the pre-emptor-petitioners and the seller Md. Shahidul Islam got the said 14 acres of the case plot No. 274 by inheritance and they had been on joint possession of 14 acres in the case plot; that while the seller, Md. Shahidul Islam, son of the pre-emptor-petitioner No.1 and brother of the pre-emptor-petitioner Nos.2 and 3 had been owning and possessing 14 acres of land of the case plot in ejmali along with the pre-emptee respondent, a stranger to the case plot by a sale deed dated 03.07.1995 of TK. 60,000.00 without the knowledge of the pre-emptor-petitioners and that the pre-emptor-petitioners are co-sharers by inheritance in the case plot and as such they filed the pre-emption. 

 3. The pre-emptee-respondent contested the pre-emption case by filing written objections contending, inter alia, that the Md. Shahed Ali, predecessor of the pre-emptor-petitioners and seller, Md. Shaidul Islam, had 14 annas share and Saheran, mother of the said Md. Shahed Ali had 2 annas share in 14 acres of the case plot and accordingly S.A. Khatian No. 131 was finally published; that afterwards the said Shaeran died leaving behind son, Md. Shahed Ali, by amicable partition amongst the heirs of the said Md. Shahed Ali, the seller, Md. Shahidul Islam got the entire 14 acres of the plot and had been in possession of the same; that the seller, Md. Shahidul Islam requested the other co-sharers of the said Md. Shahed Ali to purchase the case land but all of them refused. Thereafter the seller, Md. Shahidul Islam requested the pre-emptee-respondent to purchase the case land who purchased the case land by a sale deed dated 03.07.1995 and he has been in possession of the case land since his purchase. Moreover, the pre-emptee-respondent made construction in the case land before the receipt of notice of the case.
